article_text:
Many books will provide backbone to both theatrical and streaming releases in 2026.

From the long-awaited rom com film adaptation of Emily Henry’s People We Meet on Vacation , which hit Netflix in January, to the Ridley Scott-directed adaptation of The Dog Stars starring Jacob Elordi, Josh Brolin and Margaret Qualley that arrived in August, several major releases will come off the page and to life on the big screen.

Related Stories

30+ TV Show Book Adaptations Arriving This Year So Far

Which Colleen Hoover Books Are Becoming Movies? ‘Verity,’ ‘Reminders Of Him’ & ‘Regretting You’ Will Join ‘It Ends With Us’

Still more films to look forward to later in the year are the adaptations of Suzanne Collins’ Hunger Games prequel novel, Sunrise on the Reaping , as well as Denis Villeneuve’s third Dune film. Netflix has some holiday book adaptations coming at the end of the year as well.

Find all the films based on books coming out next year below:

Watch on Deadline

The Wicker Husband by Ursula Wills-Jones

Wicker starring Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård, Elizabeth Debicki and Peter Dinklage gets a limited theatrical release Oct. 23 followed by a wide one Oct. 30.

RELATED: ‘Wicker’ Red Carpet Premiere Photos: Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård, Elizabeth Debicki & More

Klara and the Sun by Kazuo Ishiguro

The Taika Waititi-directed adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun , starring Jenna Ortega, Amy Adams, Aran Murphy and Mia Tharia will arrive in theaters Oct. 23. A first look and footage were shown at CinemaCon 2026.

Wildwood by Colin Meloy with Illustrations by Carson Ellis

Laika’s first stop-motion movie since The Missing Link (2019) is an adaptation of The Decemberists’ frontman Colin Meloy’s book Wildwood . Prue McKeel (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) lives a pretty ordinary life until her baby brother gets kidnapped by a murder of crows, leading her to launch a rescue mission in the Impassable Wilderness, an enchanted forest hidden just beyond Portland, OR. Her classmate Curtis Mehlberg (Jacob Tremblay) offers to help.

RELATED: ‘Wildwood’ Trailer: Laika Returns To Its Nature With Latest Stop-Motion Fantasy Adventure

The voice cast for the film also includes Carey Mulligan, Richard E. Grant, Awkwafina, Amandla Stenberg, Tom Waits, Charlie Day, Blythe Danner, Arthur Knight, Maya Erskine, Jake Johnson, Tantoo Cardinal, Rob Delaney, Jemaine Clement, Marc Evan Jackson, Len Cariou, Ólafur Darri Ólafsson, Angela Bassett and Mahershala Ali.

The Bodyguard by Katherine Center

Netflix’s film adaptation of Katherine Center’s The Bodyguard will arrive on the streamer November 18. The movie stars Jared Padalecki, Leighton Meester, Andi McDowell, Noah LaLonde, Toby Sandeman, Walker Hayes, CM Punk and more.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping by Suzanne Collins

In a Holidaze by Christina Lauren

Netflix has another holiday romantic comedy based on a book coming December 2. Christina Lauren’s In a Holidaze follows a Groundhog Day Christmas cabin stay that repeats as the main character is caught in a time loop. The film stars Maddie Ziegler , Rob Lowe , Graham Phillips and Elias Kacavas. Patton Oswalt, Jackie Sandler, Gil Bellows and Andrea Anders will also appear .

RELATED: ‘In A Holidaze’ Film Adaptation Of Christina Lauren’s Novel Sets Release Date At Netflix

Dune Messiah by Frank Herbert

Denis Villeneuve’s final Dune film will pick up with a large time gap after the events of the first book that Frank Herbert wrote. New cast include Robert Pattinson as the major villain as well as two youngsters, one the son of star Jason Momoa, portraying Paul Atreides and Chani’s children. The epic conclusion is headed to theaters Dec. 18 alongside Avengers: Doomsday .

Movies in the Making Based on Books:

Children of Blood and Bone by Tomi Adeyemi, Film adaptation coming to theaters in 2027 directed by Gina Prince-Bythewood, adapted by Prince-Bythewood and Adeyemi

The Magician’s Nephew by C.S. Lewis – Feature film directed by Greta Gerwig , arriving in theaters in February 2027

The Nightingale by Kristin Hannah, Feature film coming to theaters March 2027 starring Elle and Dakota Fanning

Beach Read by Emily Henry – Film Being Written, Director Yulin Kuang Attached , Phoebe Dynevor Cast as January Andrews , Patrick Schwarzenegger Cast As Gus Everett , production has wrapped

Jeré Longman’s book , The Girls of Summer: The US Women’s Soccer Team and How It Changed the World , feature adaptation coming to Netflix starring Zoey Deutch, Emily Bader, Emilia Jones & more In a Holidaze by Christina Lauren (Combined pen name of Christina Hobbs & Lauren Billings Luhrs) – In the works with Netflix with Tiffany Paulsen writing and Cast of Maddie Ziegler, Rob Lowe and more

The Bodyguard by Katherine Center – In the works at Netflix with Leighton Meester, Jared Padalecki & more

Deep Cuts by Holly Brickley, Feature film in the works with A24 starring Drew Starkey and Cailee Spaeny

The Midnight Library by Matt Haig – Florence Pugh attached to star in movie from Studiocanal and Blueprint Pictures, launching at Cannes

Book Lovers by Emily Henry – Sarah Heyward To Write Film Script for Tango

Funny Story by Emily Henry – Henry Writing Movie Script

None of This Is True by Lisa Jewell – Netflix Adapting into Film, Eleanor Burgess Writing Script

Then She Was Gone by Lisa Jewell – Film Adaptation from Crystal City Entertainment and Moonshot Films

Happy Place by Emily Henry – Originally optioned by Jennifer Lopez’s Nuyorican Productions for TV Show, but now becoming a film for Netflix

The Pearl Thief by Fiona McIntosh – Film Feature Adaptation from Made Up Stories

Some Part of Her by Amy Chozick – Feature Film Adaptation, Rights Optioned by Fifth Season

Broken Country by Clare Leslie Hall – Sony 3000 Acquired Film Rights , Hello Sunshine Producing

The Wedding Date by Jasmine Guillory – Tracy Oliver Adapting for Netflix with Prince Harry & Meghan Markle Producing

Custom of the Country by Edith Wharton, Starring Sydney Sweeney, Leo Woodall and more

Lincoln in the Bardo by George Saunders – Film Adaptation Produced and Directed by Duke Johnson with Tom Hanks starring as Lincoln

The Correspondent by Virginia Evans, Feature Adaptation in the works at Lionsgate with Jane Fonda attached, Cat Vasko penning script and Todd Lieberman’s Hidden Pictures producing

The Favorites by Layne Fargo, in development at Netflix with Welle Entertainment banner

Strangers: A Memoir of Marriage by Belle Burden, Going to Netflix starring Gwyneth Paltrow

Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke, Amazon MGM won auction before publication with Anne Hathaway attached to star , Hannah Friedman penning adaptation

A Good Person by Kirsten King – Feature adaptation with Working Title Films, King adapting script and Daisy Edgar-Jones producing

Better Than the Movies by Lynn Painter, Feature adaptation in the works at Netflix with Julia Hart ( I’m Your Woman ) directing and co-writing the project with husband and creative partner Jordan Horowitz, Beatrice Kitsos and David Iacono attached to star as lead couple

Fake Skating by Lynn Painter , Feature film adaptation in the works from Will Gluck’s Olive Bridge and Sony Pictures, to be directed by Josh Boone

Love, Theoretically by Ali Hazelwood, Feature film in the works at Prime Video with Sofia Alvarez directing and Colleen Hoovers’ Heartbones production company producing

Deep End by Ali Hazelwood, Movie adaptation in the works at Netflix with Shawn Levy’s 21 Laps & Alex Cooper’s Unwell Productions behind it

Everything Was Beautiful and Nothing Hurt by Ben Reeves – film in development with Marc Turtletaub attached to direct

Theo of Golden by Allen Levi – Warner Bros i n negotiations for rights, Tom Hanks in talks to play title character

The Life And Adventures of Santa Claus by L. Frank Baum – Kali Bailey adapting for Monarch Media

Dolly All The Time by Annabel Monaghan – Gemma Burgess adapting feature with Sony 3000 Pictures and Temple Hill behind it

Paradox Inc. by Forrest Brazeal – Daniel Roher and Lord Miller set to produce for Universal Pictures

The Dallergut Dream Department Store by Miye Lee – Disney Live Action developing feature adaptation

Stag Dance by Torrey Peters – Run-A-Muck developing

The Final Girl Support Group by Grady Hendrix – Adapted by Christopher Landon for Paramount

RELATED: Emily Henry Adapting ‘Funny Story’ Novel Into Feature Film With Lyrical Media and Ryder Picture Company

Films, based on books, that arrived earlier this year (2026):

People We Meet on Vacation by Emily Henry

Brett Haley directed the movie, which will star Tom Blyth, Emily Bader, Lucien Laviscount, Molly Shannon, Alan Ruck, Miles Heizer and many more. The rom com arrives on Netflix Jan. 9.

RELATED: Everything We Know About The ‘People We Meet On Vacation’ Movie So Far

Wuthering Heights by Emily Brontë

Though many question whether this film will actually be a true adaptation or more of Cathy’s (Margo Robbie) dream world of sorts, Emerald Fennel’s blockbuster adaptation has drawn much attention and criticism for its avoidance of casting a person of color in the role of Heathcliff (Jacob Elordi). The film arrives in theaters Feb. 13 , just in time for Valentine’s Day.

Sony Pictures Animation’s ‘GOAT’ – Based on Chris Tougas’ Unpublished Funky Dunks

Sony Animation’s GOAT , which stars a voice cast of Caleb McLaughlin, Gabrielle Union, Nicola Coughlan, David Harbour, Stephen Curry and more, is inspired by Funky Dunks written by Chris Tougas.

Midwinter Break by Bernard MacLaverty

Bernard MacLaverty’s novel has been adapted into a Focus Features film starring Lesley Manville and Ciarán Hinds. They play a retired couple who take a trip to Amsterdam, which brings up past feelings that challenge them. The film arrives in theaters Feb. 20.

Reminders of Him by Colleen Hoover

The Colleen Hoover book-to-movie adaptations continue with Reminders of Him starring Maika Monroe, Rudy Pankow, Tyriq Withers, Lauren Graham and more. The film is equal parts love story and tragedy as Monroe’s character grapples with a decision that cost her a lot and put her in prison. Reminders of Him hits theaters March 13 .

Project Hail Mary by Andy Weir

From the author of The Martian came Project Hail Mary , which has come to life in a film starring Ryan Gosling as Ryland Grace, a teacher forced to become an astronau t in an eleventh hour attempt to save Earth from a dying sun. The film also stars Sandra Hüller, Lionel Boyce, Ken Leung and Milana Vayntrub.

The Pout-Pout Fish by Deborah Diesen with Pictures by Dan Hannah

Nick Offerman will voice the titular blue fish in the Richard Cussó-directed The Pout-Pout Fish , which swims into theaters March 20.

The Devil Wears Prada by Lauren Weisberger

While sequel film The Devil Wears Prada 2 will likely diverge somewhat from Weisberger’s novel that inspired the 2006 film. There were more books that Weisberger wrote, including Revenge Wears Prada: The Devil Returns . The followup film will hit theaters May 1.

RELATED: Everything We Know About ‘The Devil Wears Prada 2’

Animal Farm by George Orwell

Andy Serkis directed the animated Animal Farm film based on George Orwell’s novella. The film, which stars a voice cast of Seth Rogen, Glenn Close, Gatan Matarazzo, Iman Vellani and many more — arrives in theaters May 1.

Remarkably Bright Creatures by Shelby Van Pelt

Shelby Van Pelt’s beloved octopus story Remarkably Bright Creatures , directed and co-written by Olivia Newman, stars Sally Field, Lewis Pullman, Colm Meaney and more. Alfred Molina will voice Marcellus, the main octopus. The feature adaptation arrived on Netflix May 8 .

RELATED: How ‘Remarkably Bright Creatures’ Director Olivia Newman Established CGI “Protagonist” Octopus Narrator And Met Request Of “More Marcellus” Upon Delivering Film’s First Cut

Three Bags Full by Leonie Swann

Based on the novel Three Bags Full by Leonie Swann, The Sheep Detectives comes from Craig Mazin’s screenplay and story and is directed by Kyle Balda. The film arrives in theaters May 8, and it stars Hugh Jackman, Nicholas Braun, Nicholas Galitzine, Molly Gordon, Hong Chau, Emma Thompson, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Chris O’Dowd, Regina Hall, Patrick Stewart, Bella Ramsey, Brett Goldstein and Rhys Darby.

Jackman plays George, a shepherd who reads detective novels to his sheep every night. Though he doesn’t think they could possibly understand what goes on in those books, the sheep apply what they’ve learned after something happens on the farm.

Masters of the Universe

Masters of the Universe starring Nicholas Galitzine and Camila Mendes, has roots in comic books as well as the Mattel action figure. The film arrives in June.

Homer’s The Odyssey

Christopher Nolan’s rendition of The Odyssey will arrive in theaters July 17. It stars Matt Damon as Odysseus, Anne Hathaway as Penelope, Tom Holland as Telemachus and many more.

Heartstopper Forever by Alice Oseman

The film conclusion to Netflix’s live-action Heartstopper television series arrives July 17 on Netflix. Its source material, Oseman’s sixth and final graphic novel in her best-selling series, arrives July 2, 2026.

RELATED: ‘Heartstopper Forever’: Nick & Charlie Prepare For Long Distance In Trailer For Netflix Finale

The Magic Faraway Tree by Enid Blyton

Andrew Garfield, Claire Foy, Nicola Coughlan, Jessica Gunning, Rebecca Ferguson and more lead the Vertical-acquired Magic Faraway tree film adaptation, coming to theaters August 21. The film also stars Nonso Anozie, Jennifer Saunders, Hiran Abeysekara and Pippa Bennett-Warner.

The Last Sunrise by Anna Todd

Anna Todd’s The Last Sunrise has been adapted into a film for Prime Video starring Maia Reficco, Fernando Lindez, Eva Longoria and more. The movie arrives on the streamer August 26. Screenwriter Anna Klassen adapted the first book, and Amazon MGM is eyeing a sequel to the film based on a new novel by Todd, who plans to publish a trilogy.

The Dog Stars by Peter Heller

Jacob Elordi, Josh Brolin, Margaret Qualley and more will star in The Dog Stars , directed by Ridley Scott and adapted from Peter Heller’s novel. The post-apocalyptic setting occurs due to a flu plague that wiped out America. Elordi plays a pilot living with an ex-marine. The film was pushed from late March to August 28, 2026.

RELATED: Jacob Elordi & Josh Brolin Navigate “Kill Or Be Killed” Post-Apocalyptic World In Final Trailer For ‘The Dog Stars’

The Whisper Man by Alex North

Alex North’s bestselling thriller The Whisper Man film adaptation will arrive on Netflix August 28. Starring Adam Scott, Robert De Niro and Michelle Monaghan, the story watches a widowed crime writer reach out to his estranged father after his son is kidnapped. The father is a former police detective, now retired, and they make the disturbing connection that the abduction may be connected to convicted serial killer, “The Whisper Man.” James Ashcroft ( The Rule of Jenny Pen ) directed from a script by Ben Jacoby and Chase Palmer, with Hamish Linklater, Owen Teague, Acston Luca Porto, and Will Brill rounding out the cast.

The Book of Magic by Alice Hoffman

Practical Magic 2 , hitting theaters Sept. 11, 2026, will be based on The Book of Magic, the sequel to Alice Hoffman’s first Practical Magic book, producer Denise Di Novi told Entertainment Weekly . Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bulllock will return alongside Dianne West and Stockard Channing. Joey King, Lee Pace, Maisie Williams, Xolo Maridueña and Solly McLeod are newcomers for the sequel film.

RELATED: 5 Big Differences Between ‘Practical Magic 2’ And Alice Hoffman’s ‘The Book Of Magic’

The Love Hypothesis by Ali Hazelwood

Lili Reinhart and Tom Bateman will star in Prime Video’s film adaptation of The Love Hypothesis, coming to the streamer Sept. 23. A trailer has been released . Based on the book by Ali Hazelwood, the story contains the fake-dating trope and some science.

RELATED: Everything We Know About ‘The Love Hypothesis’ Movie So Far

Verity by Colleen Hoover

Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson and Josh Hartnett will lead the film adaptation of Colleen Hoover’s Verity , a thriller story that stands apart from the other three of her books that got the big screen treatment. The film arrives in theaters Oct. 2, 2026.

RELATED: Everything We Know About Amazon’s ‘Verity’ Movie So Far

Sense And Sensibility by Jane Austen

Following in the footsteps of the 1995 adaptation of Jane Austen’s novel, Focus Features will present a new take on the classic starring Daisy Edgar-Jones, Esmé Creed-Miles, Caitríona Balfe, Frank Dillane, Fiona Shaw and many more. The film arrives in theaters Oct. 16, 2026. The trailer is now available to watch.

Whalefall by Daniel Kraus

Starring Austin Abrams and Josh Brolin, Whalefall , based on the book by Daniel Kraus, will swim into theaters Oct. 16 as well. Brian Duffield directed the film from a script he co-wrote with Kraus. The film follows the story of a son who scuba dives for his father’s remains and gets swallowed by a sperm whale in the process.

RELATED: How ‘Whalefall’s Director & Author Wove The Closure Of A Father-Son Relationship Into A Survival Tale

Find book adaptation films that came out in 2025 below:

Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy by Helen Fielding – February 14, 2025

Bridget Jones (Renée Zellweger) returns in the fourth film, based on the book of the same name by Helen Fielding, after three previous installments: Bridget Jones’s Diary (2001), Bridget Jones: The Edge of Reason (2004) and Bridget Jones’s Baby (2016). Leo Woodall ( The White Lotus, One Day ) and Chiwetel Eijofor ( Rob Peace , Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness ) will star as newcomers to the franchise. Isla Fisher ( Wedding Crashers ), Josette Simon ( Anatomy of a Scandal ), Nico Parker ( Suncoast , How to Train Your Dragon ) and Leila Farzad ( I Hate Suzie ) are also set to appear.

RELATED: New Bridget Jones Film Is “Very Sad,” Hugh Grant Reveals

Mickey7 by Edward Ashton – Theaters – March 7, 2025

Bong Joon Ho has directed an adaptation of Edward Ashton’s Mickey7 titled Mickey 17 because Robert Pattinson’s titular Expendable, who dies ten more times than in Ashton’s book according Bong, hence the title change. Mickey is sought out to help colonize Niflheim, an ice world, on a suicidal mission, as demonstrated in the film’s trailer . Naomi Ackie ( Star Wars: Episode IX – The Rise of Skywalker ), Steven Yeun ( Beef ), Toni Collette ( Hereditary ), and Mark Ruffalo ( Poor Things ) will also star in the film from the Parasite director.

The Electric State by Simon Stålenhag – Netflix, March 14

Netflix’s feature film adaptation of The Electric State was directed by Anthony and Joe Russo. It stars Millie Bobby Brown as Michelle and Chris Pratt as Keats, in addition to Stanley Tucci, Giancarlo Esposito and Key Huy Quan. The robots are voiced by Brian Cox, Anthony Mackie, Woody Harrelson and Jenny Slate, to name a few.

The Life List by Lori Nelson Spielman – Netflix – March 28

Netflix’s The Life List is based on the book by Lori Nelson Spielman. Alex (Carson) has a great life, a good job and a longtime boyfriend, but when her mother (Connie Britton) dies after a second wave of cancer, Alex’s perspective shifts. Her mom leaves her beind prompts from her life list, executed by Brad (Kyle Allen) to help Alex get back on track and live a life she loves.

The Friend by Sigrid Nunez – Theaters – April 4, 2025

Naomi Watts stars in Bleecker Street’s film adaptation of Sigrid Nunez’s The Friend , which she wrote about a bond with a Great Dane. The film also stars Bill Murray, Carla Gugino, Constance Wu, Sarah Pidgeon, Noma Dumezweni and more.

On Swift Horses – Theaters – April

Daisy Edgar-Jones, Jacob Elordi and Will Poulter star in On Swift Horses , based on the book by Shannon Pufahl. The film is directed by Daniel Minahan ( Deadwood: The Movie) , and the story follows Muriel (Edgar-Jones) and her husband Lee (Poulter) as they are beginning a bright new life in California upon Lee’s return from the Korean War. Elordi plays Julius, a wayward gambler with a secret past. The adaptation hits theaters April 25.

My Oxford Year by Julia Whelan – Netflix – August 1, 2025

After previously appearing in another Netflix film based on a book, The Life List earlier this year, Sofia Carson’s next project, My Oxford Year , based on the book by Julia Whelan, will arrive on the streamer August 1. Carson will portray Anna De La Vega, who studies at Oxford University for a graduate program before returning to the U.S. for a high-paying job at Goldman Sachs that she has already secured. However, a spark with her poetry professor Jamie Davenport (Corey Mylchreest) could throw all those plans to the wind.

The Thursday Murder Club by Richard Osman – Netflix – August 28, 2025

Netflix’s The Thursday Murder Club , based on the book by Richard Osman from director Chris Columbus , will arrive on the streamer August 28. The film will star the core four characters from Osman’s book: Elizabeth (Helen Mirren), Ron (Pierce Brosnan), Ibrahim (Ben Kingsley) and Joyce (Celia Imrie) as well as Naomi Ackie, Daniel Mays, Henry Lloyd-Hughes, Tom Ellis, Jonathan Pryce, David Tennant, Paul Freeman, Geoff Bell, Richard E. Grant and Ingrid Oliver. The titular quartet spend their time solving cold case murders for fun until an unexplained death occurs in their territory, they take their casual sleuthing to the next level to solve the whodunnit.

Caught Stealing by Charlie Huston – Theaters – Aug. 29, 2025

Darren Aronofskey’s Caught Stealing is based on the book by Charlie Huston. The film, starring Austin Butler, Zoë Kravitz, Matt Smith Regina King and more arrived in theaters August 29. Hank Thompson (Butler) is asked by his neighbor Russ (Smith) to watch Bud the cat, but he unfortunately gets caught up in Russ’ business, which complicates his life significantly. Kravitz plays Hank’s girlfriend.

The Long Walk by Stephen King – Theaters – Sept. 12, 2025

Stephen King’s The Long Walk has been adapted into a feature film directed by Francis Lawrence ( Catching Fire, Mockingjay Parts 1 and 2 and The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes ). The dystipian horror novel came out in 1979, initially published under King’s pseudonym Richard Bachman. The film will star Cooper Hoffman ( Licorice Pizza ), David Jonsson ( Alien: Romulus ), Garrett Wareing ( Ransom Canyon, Manifest ), Charlie Plummer ( Looking for Alaska ) and Mark Hamill ( The Life of Chuck ). The title refers to an exercise similar to The Hunger Games in which 50 teenage boys compete to walk at a pace of 3 miles forever without rest until only one remains.

Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another – Vineland by Thomas Pynchon

Paul Thomas Anderson’s latest film, One Battle After Another , is loosely based on Thomas Pynchon’s novel Vineland . Anderson wrote the screenplay for the film, which stars Leonardo DiCaprio, Teyana Taylor, Sean Penn, Benicio Del Toro, Regina Hall, Chase Infiniti and more.

The Woman in Cabin 10 by Ruth Ware – Netflix – Oct. 10, 2025

Ruth Ware’s The Woman in Cabin 10, is getting a film adaptation starring Kiera Knightly, Guy Pearce, Hannah Waddingham, David Ajala, David Morrissey, Gugu Mbatha-Raw, Kaya Scodelario, Gitte Witt, Art Malik, Daniel Ings, Christopher Rygh, Paul Kaye, Lisa Loven Kongsli, John Macmillan, Pippa Bennett-Warner and Ayọ̀ Owóyẹmi-Peters. The story follows a journalist who sees a cruise passenger get tossed overboard one night, only to be told she dreamed the scenario and that all passengers are accounted for the next day. Her search for answers and suspicion will lead her on a twisty path that puts her own in danger. Ware recently published a sequel to The Woman in Cabin 10 , The Woman in Suite 11 .

Frankenstein by Mary Shelley – Theaters Oct. 17 & Streaming on Netflix Starting Nov. 7

Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein will get two adaptations this year, with Maggie Gyllenhaal’s The Bride opening in theaters in September while Guillermo Del Toro’s adaptation for Netflix is slated for some time this year. Gyllenhaal’s film follows Christian Bale’s lonely Frankenstein, who ventures to Chicago in the 1930s to ask Dr. Euphronius for help in creating a companion for himself. The two reanimate a murdered young woman, and an explosive romance ensues catching the attention of society. Del Toro’s adaptation will star Jacob Elordi, Christoph Waltz, Felix Kammerer, Lars Mikkelsen, David Bradley and Christian Convery. Deadline broke the news of Oscar Isaac’s role as Victor Frankenstein, and that Mia Goth is also set to star in the pic. Andrew Garfield was originally playing the role that Elordi now has — that of Frankenstein’s monster.

Regretting You by Colleen Hoover – Theaters – Oct. 24, 2025

Paramount’s film adaptation of a Colleen Hoover book, Regretting You , starring Allison Williams, Mckenna Grace, Dave Franco and Mason Thames will arrive in theaters in October. Josh Boone ( The Fault in Our Stars ) will direct from Susan McMartin’s ( After ) script. The film comes from Constantin Film, whose Robert Kulzer is set to produce along with Brunson Green and Anna Todd. The story follows Morgan Grant (Williams), who became a mother at a young age, and her daughter, Clara (Grace). Morgan struggles with putting her ambitions on pause to raise Clara, and their relationship gets stretched after a tragic accident takes the life of Clara’s father and Morgan’s husband Chris which further complicates the tension of Clara being a teenager. Franco will portray Morgan’s love interest Jonah, who she meets after Chris’ death.

RELATED: ‘Regretting You’ Trailer: Allison Williams & Mckenna Grace Star As Mother And Daughter In Paramount’s Colleen Hoover Adaptation

Train Dreams – Select Theaters Nov. 7, on Netflix Nov. 21

Train Dreams, directed by Clint Bentley is an adaptation of the novella by Denis Johnson. The script was co-written by Bentley and Greg Kwedar. The story follows Robert Grainier (Joel Edgerton) who works in the forests of the Pacific Northwest to expand America’s railroad. Felicity Jones plays his sweetheart and eventual wife, Gladys. The film also stars William H. Macy and Kerry Condon. Nathaniel Arcand and Alfred Hsing also appear, and Will Patton serves as the narrator.

The Running Man by Stephen King – Theaters – Nov. 14, 2025

Edgar Wright has written and directed a film adaptation of Stephen King’s The Running Man for Paramount. Glen Powell will star in the film, which is produced by Nira Park and Simon Kinberg. King originally published the novel under the pseudonym Richard Bachman, and the story of a futuristic America and dystopian society set in the year 2025 has already been adapted into an 1987 film starring Arnold Schwarzenegger.

RELATED: ‘The Running Man’ Trailer: Glen Powell Leads Edgar Wright’s Latest

Wicked: For Good – Theaters – Nov. 23, 2025

The second part of Jon M. Chu’s Wicked film adaptation will arrive a year after its first half made magic at the box office ahead of Thanksgiving 2024. The second half of the film will pick up after the rousing rendition of “Defying Gravity” performed by Cynthia Erivo at the end of the first film as she flew to the Western skies. Erivo has also recently hinted of an original song she wrote for the film.

RELATED: Wicked: For Good’ Trailer Pits Elphaba Vs. Glinda In Battle For Oz: “There’s No Going Back”

Hamnet by Maggie O’Farrell – Theaters – Nov. 27 Limited, Wide Release December 12

Maggie O’Farrell’s Hamnet is getting a feature film adaptation treatment from Eternals and Nomadland director Chloe Zhao. Zhao cowrote the film, from Focus Features, with O’Farrell, whose book tells a powerful love story based on Shakespeare’s play Hamlet . The film will star Jessie Buckley, Paul Mescal, Emily Watson and Joe Alwyn. Producers are Liza Marshall, Pippa Harris, Nic Gonda, Sam Mendes and Steven Spielberg on behalf of Amblin. EPs are Kristie Macosko Krieger on behalf of Amblin, Laurie Borg and Zhao. The book came out in 2020.

The Housemaid by Frieda McFadden – Christmas Day 2025

Paul Feig’s The Housemaid feature film adaptation of Frieda McFadden’s book will star Sydney Sweeney, Amanda Seyfried and Brandon Sklenar. Adapted by Rebecca Sonnenshine, the film will release in theaters Dec. 25 , 2025 alongside Timothée Chalamet’s Marty Supreme . Michele Morrone, who also stars in Feig’s Another Simple Favor followup to A Simple Favor (2018), will appear in The Housemaid as well.

article_text:
Netflix ’s flurry of C-suite changes ( Peter Rice in, Bela Bajaria and others out) along with its deepest round of layoffs since 2022 are setting the company on a new path – but to where?

That’s the question Wall Street is asking as the company preps its latest quarterly earnings and investor call set for after Tuesday’s stock market close.

Related Stories

Netflix Shakeup: Peter Rice Is Welcomed Back To Executive Ranks While Bela Bajaria’s Exit Has Layoff-Weary Staff Bracing For More Upheaval

Ted Sarandos Shrugs Off U.S. Troubles To Mark Netflix’s 10 Years In Korea

Investors “need, in short order, some indications toward confidence in the growth trajectory that this powerful, global platform should be able to provide,” said David Joyce of Seaport Research Partners. He and others suggest more live sports, a laser focus on advertising, expanded third-party partnerships, continued experimentation with theatrical releasing, and perhaps another stab at M&A once NBCUniversal is spun out.

Watch on Deadline

The Street is eager for insights around viewer engagement and the upcoming original content slate, both Achilles’ heels of late. Coming on the heels of the Skydance merger close , which established Netflix as the bridesmaid in the pursuit of Warner Bros., this will be the giant streamer’s most consequential earnings report in years. Its stock, in part due to the questions prompted by the Warner chase, has been slumping, with shares down 25% year to date and over 40% over the past 12 months.

The roughly 1,000 job cuts, or 6% of staff, reached to the heights of the org chart. Film head Dan Lin was ousted earlier Monday, on the heels of his lieutenant Doug Belgrad and content chief Bajaria, a 10-year veteran. She was replaced by former Disney and Fox executive Peter Rice as Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters are “structuring the narrative for the earnings call and beyond,” Joyce observed.

Analysts are eyeing revenue of $12.8 billion for the three months ended September 30, up 11.8% from the year-earlier quarter, with earnings per share of 82 cents vs. 59 cents. But the numbers – assuming they’re in line with expectations – may be less critical than commentary by Sarandos and Peters. The former was particularly candid at a recent Bloomberg conference, saying v iewership was not growing as much as he would like .

Investors (and Hollywood players) were taken aback by the company’s Warner Bros bid, and have also noted that the summer did not see a seasonal rebound in engagement. Record-breaking FIFA World Cup telecasts ate into the overall market, but even so, “fewer Netflix titles are capturing the highest levels of streaming engagement” as competition for time and attention continues to intensify, Matthew Condon of Citizens wrote in a client note. With the layoffs , he added, “we believe the company is strategically realigning spend behind its highest priority initiatives as it looks to improve engagement and revenue growth.”

He has a “market perform” rating on the stock (essentially a hold) “as we await a more definitive set of catalysts that we believe are capable of driving sustained upward estimate revisions.”

Joyce said in a recent report that the shares are so low he recommends a “buy” but did lower his price target to $90 from $102. The stock is “in somewhat of a ‘show-me’, wait-and-see period.”

TD Cowen’s John Blackledge also has a “buy” on the streamer with a $100 price target. He thinks Netflix will be able to lift engagement and drive member growth and retention with “emerging engagement vectors” from live sports to podcasts. “We expect solid 3Q26 results and believe NFLX can sustain its intermediate-term financial objectives, incl. healthy top-line growth, margin expansion and rising FCF [free cash flow].”

M&A is now on the table, certainly after the pursuit of Paramount upended more than a quarter century of aversion to major acquisitions for Netflix, which now ranks sixth in U.S. TV usage, pro forma for the Skydance and pending Fox-Roku mergers, says Joyce. A significant leapfrog in market share could come from an acquisition of NBCUniversal, which will be spun out from Comcast next year, taking the streamer from 7.8% to 14.9%.

Rice, now chief content officer at Netflix, “has a significant skill set in managing sports and entertainment programming for both 20th Century Fox and Disney, after the latter acquired the former, and therefore has experience with merging two companies’ content/programming operations, which could be useful,” he notes.

Sports rights are key as Netflix competes for subscribers and advertising with rivals from DAZN to Amazon, Apple and YouTube. Netflix closed its 2026 upfront in August with advertising commitments nearly doubling on strong demand for live including the NFL, WWE, MLB and 2027 Women’s World Cup The streamer just acquired Spanish and Andorran rights to all 104 matches of the 2030 men’s FIFA World Cup.

Third-party content partnerships and integrations are potentially attractive near-term catalysts, particularly with the likes of Peacock or Fox One that could bring premium live sports onto the platform without significant upfront rights investment, said Condon.

Sarandos has also pointed to Netflix’s TF1 partnership in France as a new and promising model.

And the importance of Netflix’s advertising execution is rising, noted Joyce. Rounds of streaming price hikes are nudging more viewers to cheaper ad tiers, with significant international growth potential. The connected TV market is growing. So is the ad market for creator and short-form video, another potential growth area for the streamer. It could also simply add more inventory.

Netflix has forecast $3 billion in ad revenue for this year.

In theatrical, the streamer this past weekend started a major experiment with much longer windows and official box office reporting. It opened award-winning Spanish film La Bola Negra in limited release with a 45-day window and has a handful of others, including high-profile wide releases, teed up for cinemas.

Management has been wary of calling this a strategy shift and appears focused on evaluating each film individually, balancing demand from moviegoers with the potential impact on Netflix viewing, Condon noted. He believes theatrical releases can help build greater fandom around Netflix IP and boost the platform — a case that theater owners have been pressing for years.

"苏泽特·贝尔-罗伯茨：“马永加”（Manyonga）始于神经可塑性——大脑通过经验和改变自我重组的能力。是什么促使你将这一科学理念转化为展览的策展框架？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "法德扎伊·维罗尼卡·穆切姆瓦：我对神经可塑性感兴趣的，未必是孤立的科学本身，而是它为思考我们如何成为今天的自己所开启的哲学可能性。大脑并非固定结构的观点——即它在不断响应经验进行自我重组——为思考艺术实践、记忆以及塑造身份的社会条件提供了一种引人入胜的方式。我们倾向于将转化想象为单一事件，即某种根本改变发生后的决裂。但神经可塑性表明了一些更复杂的事情：转化往往是累积的，通过重复、遭遇、中断以及我们在继承与体验之间不断进行的协商而发生。我开始以类似的方式思考艺术实践。艺术家们不断地使用积累的经验、继承的视觉语言、材料、记忆和历史。他们重访、拆解和重建这些元素，有时是有意识的，有时是直觉的。因此，展览成为一个探索经验与转化之间关系的契机，并探讨我们所谓的“第二自然”是否曾经完全定型。我也对抵制“适应必然是积极的”这一假设很感兴趣。改变的能力并不意味着要求改变的环境是公正或可取的。有时，适应是对暴力、流离失所或动荡不安的回应。这种张力成为了展览概念框架的重要部分。吉迪恩·戈莫，《一个人的观众》（Audience of One），2025年。2026年威尼斯双年展上的“第二自然 | 马永加”。摄影：苏泽特·贝尔-罗伯茨（Suzette Bell-Roberts）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-22-at-12.52.17-1017x1030.png", "alt": "", "caption": "吉迪恩·戈莫，《一个人的观众》（Audience of One），2025年。2026年威尼斯双年展上的“第二自然 | 马永加”。摄影：苏泽特·贝尔-罗伯茨（Suzette Bell-Roberts）。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“马永加”（Manyonga）引入了关于弯曲、扭转和适应的更具文化和语言特异性的概念。这个词如何使“第二自然”的概念变得更加复杂或得到延伸？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我认为“Manyonga”为展览的标题引入了一种富有成效的张力。该词具有多重含义。它可译为抵抗、根茎状的运动、手臂或拥抱，强调了连接与关系性。“Manyonga”还让人联想到骨骼、碎片或残存事物的剩余建筑，并引入了一种对位，坚守物质的痕迹以及那些拒绝消失的东西。虽然“Second Nature”暗示了通过重复变得习惯性、内化或几乎是本能的东西，并指向结构的沉积——暴力、适应和生存如何变成具身的、排练的、甚至是陈腐的——但“Manyonga”则将我们的注意力引向此类转变赖以发生的运动和协商。你对弯曲、扭转和适应这一概念的诠释，正是对展览所极力探讨的这些思想的延伸。关于弯曲和扭转，有一种特别引人深思之处，因为这些动作既暗示了灵活性又暗示了抵抗。弯曲不一定等于投降，扭转也并不总是意味着折断。知道如何在压力下做出反应包含着一种智慧，但同时也存在一个问题：在形态被不可逆转地改变之前，某物能够承受多大的压力。对我而言，“Manyonga”使我们能够将适应视为一个具身的、植根于特定文化的进程，而不是一种抽象的或普遍的人类能力。它将运动、即兴创作、甚至某种不守规矩的特质引入了更为人熟知的“第二自然”概念中。重要的是，我不希望该词仅仅充当西方科学概念的某种本土翻译。我希望这两个观念能够处于对话之中，有时相互强固，有时产生摩擦。展览要求我们思考认识转变的不同途径，无论是通过科学、语言、艺术实践还是生活经验。菲利克斯·舒姆巴（Felix Shumba），《Wheel-telegram-east-window-line 145XV7-lower》，2025年。第二自然 | Manyonga，2026年威尼斯双年展。摄影：苏赞·贝尔-罗伯茨（Suzette Bell-Roberts）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_9646-1030x490.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "菲利克斯·舒姆巴（Felix Shumba），《Wheel-telegram-east-window-line 145XV7-lower》，2025年。第二自然 | Manyonga，2026年威尼斯双年展。摄影：苏赞·贝尔-罗伯茨（Suzette Bell-Roberts）。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本次展览汇集了弗兰克兰·德辛盖（Franklyn Dzingai）、吉迪恩·戈莫（Gideon Gomo）、帕尔东·马庞代拉（Pardon Mapondera）、埃娃·拉特（Eva Raath）和菲利克斯·舒姆巴（Felix Shumba），他们的艺术实践有着显著的差异。你在他们的作品中注意到了什么，从而让你觉得这五位艺术家对于这个展览而言是必不可少的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我希望能将那些在形式上不一定相似、但对转变过程有着持续投入的艺术家聚集在一起。吸引我关注这五位艺术家的原因，恰恰在于他们从不同的立场出发来探讨材料、记忆、身份和变化等问题。我不希望办这样一个展览：其中每件作品都在阐释相同的策展主张。我希望艺术家们使这一主张变得更加复杂，并在某些情况下对其提出挑战。因此，比起确定一种共同的美学，展览更在于认识到一种对形式、意义和经验之不稳定性共同具备的敏感性。每一种实践都带来了对重塑某物意味着什么的独特理解——无论这“某物”是一种材料、一个图像、一段记忆、一种叙事，还是一种继承的世界观。他们的差异是必不可少的，因为适应并非一种单一的体验。它是参差不齐的、偶然的，并由个人和群体所处特定环境塑造。将这些艺术家聚集在一起，使展览得以抵制对转变的单一定义。从这个意义上说，展览本身就成了一次关系性思考的练习。这些作品并不被要求彼此赞同。它们的差异正是产生意义的一部分。“第二自然 | Manyonga”在第61届威尼斯双年展上的展览现场，2026年。摄影：苏赞·贝尔-罗伯茨（Suzette Bell-Roberts）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_9651-4-1030x773.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "“第二自然 | Manyonga”在第61届威尼斯双年展上的展览现场，2026年。摄影：苏赞·贝尔-罗伯茨（Suzette Bell-Roberts）。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在整个展馆中，转变不仅在概念上发生，也在物质上发生，通过切割、编织、组装、分层和重新加工来实现。材料的这种物理转化对于你关于适应和变化的思考有多重要？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "物质转化对我的思考绝对至关重要，因为它使展览概念上的关切变得切实可见。我感兴趣的是，艺术家创作作品的过程本身如何能够成为思考适应的一种方式。这些材料参与了意义的生产。它们的历史、属性、阻力和可能性，对于我们理解这些作品而言是不可或缺的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "以弗兰克林·丁盖（Franklyn Dzingai）的减法版画创作过程为例，图像是通过逐步去除材料而显现出来的。创作图像同时涉及一个不可逆的减法行为，这一点颇具引人深思之处。在帕顿·马蓬德拉（Pardon Mapondera）的作品中，被丢弃的材料被重新组合成错综复杂的构图，挑战了我们赋予物体的价值方式。伊娃·拉思（Eva Raath）对纺织品、图案和版画的运用同样表明，人们可以不断地重新加工熟悉的材料和视觉语言。吉迪恩·戈莫（Gideon Gomo）的《独一无二的观众》（Audience of One）在这方面尤为引人注目，因为这些青铜头像与木炭一同呈现，标志着他从人们更为熟悉的石雕创作中做出了转变。这里有一个重要的转变，不仅是在材料之间，而且是在关于形式、永恒和转化的不同思维方式之间。青铜带有持久性和纪念碑性的联想，而木炭则暗示着燃烧、残余以及消失的可能性。它们的并置在持久之物与易受变化影响之物之间引入了一种张力。他从石雕转向青铜，也涉及从主要以减法为主的过程向加法过程的转变。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在超越石雕的同时，戈莫也展示了如何在不一定放弃其底层关切的情况下，让成熟的艺术语言受到冲击并得到拓展。菲利克斯·舒姆巴（Felix Shumba）的大幅绘画为这场对话引入了另一个引人入胜的维度。舒姆巴制作了自己绘画所用的木炭，因此转化的过程在图像出现在纸上之前很久就已经开始了。制作木炭的过程——通过火将有机物转化为能够产生图像的材料——成为了作品概念和物质生命中不可或缺的一部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个过程有着特别强大的力量：一种与燃烧和破坏相关的材料，成为了新图像和新叙事涌现的媒介。绘画的尺度进一步使木炭表面上的脆弱性变得复杂，使得这种短暂且容易受到干扰的媒介占据了令人瞩目的物质存在感。这些过程不仅仅是技术决定。它们是通过创作产生的知识形式。让我感兴趣的是材料的阻力与艺术家改造它们的愿望之间的关系。材料有其历史、局限性和可能性。它们并不总是按我们的预期表现。这正是与神经可塑性的关系变得特别有趣的地方。转化并不一定意味着放弃早期的形式。它可能涉及保留先前存在的事物的痕迹、重组现有的结构，或者在表面局限性中发现可能性。我也认为这些物质过程具有某种政治性。在一个日益全神贯注于速度、技术创新和即时生产的世界里，切割、编织、雕刻、铸造、绘画和组装这漫长而持续的劳作提醒我们，转化可以是缓慢的、重复的且要求极高的。它需要专注。弗兰克林·丁盖（Franklyn Dzingai），《姆塞贡韦工作室的充满活力的传播》（Vibrant Transmission in Musesengwe Studio），2025年。第二自然 | 马永加（Second Nature | Manyonga），威尼斯第61届国际艺术双年展（La Biennale di Venezia 2026）。图片鸣谢：苏泽特·贝尔-罗伯茨（Suzette Bell-Roberts）。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "记忆以个人、家族、历史和集体等不同形式贯穿于整个展览。展览并没有将记忆视为固定不变的，而是表明它在不断地被重构。艺术家们是如何应对这种不稳定性的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "记忆对我来说特别有趣，因为我们经常谈论它，就好像它是一个我们可以从中检索完整经验的档案。但记忆本身就是一种重构的行为。我们记住什么、忘记什么，以及我们如何叙述我们的经历，都在不断地被现在所塑造。艺术家们通过不同的策略来应对这种不稳定性。弗兰克林·丁盖对家庭照片和其他视觉来源的运用，引发了关于个人回忆与集体身份之间关系的疑问。他的图像不仅仅是对被记住经历的简单再现，而是对它们的重新配置。菲利克斯·舒姆巴的实践通过参与历史暴力、扭曲、重复和思辨可能性，引入了另一个维度。他的作品探讨了当历史碎片从熟悉的叙事中被抽离并以不同方式发声时会发生什么。与此同时，吉迪恩·戈莫的作品通过承载自身历史的材料和雕塑传统来接合文化记忆。将这些方法联系在一起的是这样一种理解：记忆从未是天真或完整的。它受到权力、图像和叙事的可用性，以及建构我们对过去理解的那些沉默的塑造。我感兴趣的是，当艺术家打断记忆表面上的权威时会发生什么。他们为歧义、矛盾和另类解释留出了空间。对我来说，这也是展览超越对适应性直接颂扬的地方。如果我们的记忆在不断地被重构，那么我们的身份也比我们想象的要更加不稳定。问题不仅在于我们如何记忆，还在于我们的记忆行为使什么样的未来成为可能。菲利克斯·舒姆巴（Felix "其中几件作品在个人经历与津巴布韦更广阔的社会及历史现实之间穿梭。您是如何在不把艺术家的创作简单归结为单一民族叙事的前提下，来处理这种关系的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是一个需要审慎对待的重要问题，尤其是在威尼斯双年展国家馆的语境下。国家馆本身就包含着一种内在矛盾：它们将艺术家汇聚在一个国家的旗号之下，然而艺术实践却很少会完全契合国家身份的边界或期待。对于那种认为来自津巴布韦的艺术家就必须解释津巴布韦，或者认为他们的作品主要应该被解读为该国政治、经济或社会状况之佐证的期待，我一直保持着警惕。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当然，艺术家并非在历史之外创作。他们的实践发端于特定的经历、环境和人际关系。但承认这些语境，与将它们视为理解作品的唯一解释，是完全两码事。我的方法是让艺术家各自的关注点和艺术语言保持在核心位置。津巴布韦是一个连接点，但它并不是他们知识或想象世界的极限。我感兴趣的是，能否将津巴布韦当代艺术呈现为一个充满多元且有时相互矛盾的立场的领域，而不是一个单一的、连贯的国家故事。展览在主题上对适应、记忆、技术和转型的关注并非津巴布韦所独有，尽管艺术家们是从特定的生活和历史处境出发来探讨这些问题的。在讨论津巴布韦艺术创作时，浪漫化坚韧（resilience）也存在着危险。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们经常被邀请去赞叹人们如何在艰难环境中依然坚持创作。在肯定这种独创性的价值之余，我认为我们也必须审视那些让这种独创性成为必要的条件。坚韧不应成为将结构性困境正常化的语言。我希望本国家馆能为复杂性留出空间，让艺术家被理解为知识和想象的创造者，而不仅仅是一个国家的代言人。埃娃·拉思（Eva Curator Fadzai Veronica Muchemwa discusses ‘Second Nature | Manyonga’ at the National Pavilion of Zimbabwe at the 61st Venice Biennale, exploring how memory, material transformation and the pressures of survival shape our capacity for change.

At the 61st Venice Biennale, In Minor Keys , Zimbabwe’s National Pavilion challenges the assumption that adaptation is inherently liberating. Curated by Fadzai Veronica Muchemwa, ‘Second Nature | Manyonga’ brings together Franklyn Dzingai, Gideon Gomo, Pardon Mapondera, Eva Raath and Felix Shumba to examine how experience, memory and material processes shape identity and transformation. Drawing on neuroplasticity and culturally situated understandings of change, the exhibition considers the relationship between resilience and the conditions that demand it. In conversation with ART AFRICA , Muchemwa reflects on the politics of adaptation, the complexities of national representation, and the possibilities of imagining what otherwise appears inevitable. Eva Raath, ‘ Checkered Memories ‘, 2025. Second Nature | Manyonga at La Biennale di Venezia 2026. Photo credit to Suzette Bell-Roberts.

Suzette Bell-Roberts: ‘Manyonga’ begins with neuroplasticity — the brain’s capacity to reorganise itself through experience and change. What led you to translate this scientific idea into the exhibition’s curatorial framework?

Fadzai Veronica Muchemwa: What interested me about neuroplasticity was not necessarily the science in isolation, but the philosophical possibilities it opens up for thinking about how we become who we are. The idea that the brain is not a fixed structure, that it is continually reorganising itself in response to experience, offered a compelling way to think about artistic practice, memory, and the social conditions through which identities are formed. We tend to imagine transformation as a singular event, a rupture after which something fundamentally changes. But neuroplasticity suggests something more complex: that transformation is often cumulative, occurring through repetition, encounters, interruptions, and the continuous negotiation between what we have inherited and what we experience. I began thinking about artistic practice in similar terms. Artists are constantly working with accumulated experiences, inherited visual languages, materials, memories, and histories. They revisit, dismantle, and reconstruct these elements, sometimes consciously and sometimes intuitively. The exhibition therefore became an opportunity to explore the relationship between experience and transformation, and to ask whether what we call our second nature is ever entirely settled. I was also interested in resisting the assumption that adaptation is necessarily positive. The capacity to change does not mean that the circumstances demanding change are just or desirable. Sometimes adaptation is a response to violence, displacement, or precarity. That tension became important to the exhibition’s conceptual framework. Gideon Gomo, ‘ Audience of One ‘, 2025. Second Nature | Manyonga at La Biennale di Venezia 2026. Photo credit to Suzette Bell-Roberts.

‘Manyonga’ introduces a more culturally and linguistically specific idea of bending, twisting and adapting. How does the term complicate or extend the idea of “second nature”?

I think ‘Manyonga’ introduces a productive tension into the exhibition’s title. The term has multiple meanings. It translates to resistance, rhizomatic movement, arms or embraces, emphasising connection and relationality. ‘Manyonga’ also evokes bones, fragments, or the residual architecture of what remains, and introduces a counterpoint, insisting on material traces, on what refuses to disappear. While ‘Second Nature’ suggests something that becomes habitual, internalised, or almost instinctive through repetition and gestures toward the sedimentation of structures- how violence, adaptation, and survival become embodied, rehearsed, even banal- ‘Manyonga’ directs our attention to the movements and negotiations through which such transformations occur. Your interpretation of the idea of bending, twisting and adapting is an extension of these ideas that the exhibition grappled with. There is something particularly evocative about bending and twisting because these movements imply both flexibility and resistance. To bend is not necessarily to surrender, and to twist is not always to break. There is an intelligence in knowing how to move in response to pressure, but there is also a question about how much pressure something can withstand before its form is irreversibly altered. For me, ‘Manyonga’ allows us to think about adaptation as an embodied and culturally situated process instead of an abstract or universal human capacity. It introduces movement, improvisation, and perhaps even a certain unruliness into the more familiar notion of second nature. Importantly, I did not want the term to function merely as a local translation of a Western scientific concept. I wanted the two ideas to exist in conversation, sometimes reinforcing one another and sometimes producing friction. The exhibition asks us to consider different ways of knowing transformation, whether through science, language, artistic practice, or lived experience. Felix Shumba, ‘ Wheel-telegram-east-window-line 145XV7-lower ‘, 2025. Second Nature | Manyonga at La Biennale di Venezia 2026. Photo credit to Suzette Bell-Roberts.

The exhibition brings together Franklyn Dzingai, Gideon Gomo, Pardon Mapondera, Eva Raath and Felix Shumba, whose practices are markedly different. What did you recognise in their work that made these five artists necessary to this exhibition?

I was interested in bringing together artists whose practices did not necessarily resemble one another formally but who shared a sustained engagement with processes of transformation. What drew me to these five artists was precisely the fact that they approach questions of material, memory, identity, and change from different positions. I did not want an exhibition in which every work illustrated the same curatorial proposition. I wanted the artists to complicate the proposition and, in some instances, challenge it. The exhibition is therefore less about identifying a common aesthetic than about recognising a shared sensitivity to the instability of forms, meanings, and experiences. Each practice brings a different understanding of what it means to remake something, whether that something is a material, an image, a memory, a narrative, or an inherited way of seeing the world. Their differences were necessary because adaptation is not a singular experience. It is uneven, contingent, and shaped by the particular circumstances in which individuals and communities find themselves. Bringing these artists together allowed the exhibition to resist a single definition of transformation. In that sense, the exhibition itself becomes an exercise in relational thinking. The works are not required to agree with one another. Their differences are part of what generates meaning. Installation view of ‘Second Nature | Manyonga’ at the 61st Biennale di Venezia, 2026. Photo credit to Suzette Bell-Roberts.

Across the Pavilion, transformation happens not only conceptually but materially, through cutting, weaving, assembling, layering, and reworking. How important was this physical transformation of materials to your thinking about adaptation and change?

Material transformation was absolutely central to my thinking because it allowed the exhibition’s conceptual concerns to become tangible. I was interested in how the processes through which artists make their work could themselves become ways of thinking about adaptation. The materials participate in the production of meaning. Their histories, properties, resistance, and possibilities are integral to how we understand the works.

Consider Franklyn Dzingai’s reductive printmaking process, in which an image emerges through the progressive removal of material. There is something compelling about the fact that making an image also involves an irreversible act of subtraction. With Pardon Mapondera, discarded materials are reconstituted into intricate compositions that challenge how we assign value to objects. Eva Raath’s engagement with textiles, patterns, and printmaking similarly demonstrates how familiar materials and visual languages can be continually reworked. Gideon Gomo’s Audience of One is particularly interesting in this regard because the bronze heads, presented alongside charcoal, mark a departure from his more familiar stone sculptural practice. There is an important shift here, not simply between materials but between different ways of thinking about form, permanence, and transformation. Bronze carries associations of durability and monumentality, while charcoal suggests combustion, residue, and the possibility of disappearance. Their juxtaposition introduces a tension between what endures and what remains vulnerable to change. His movement from stone carving to bronze also involves a shift from a predominantly subtractive process to an additive one.

In moving beyond stone, Gomo also demonstrates how an established artistic language can be unsettled and expanded without necessarily abandoning its underlying concerns. Felix Shumba’s large-scale drawings introduce another compelling dimension to this conversation. Shumba makes the charcoal with which he draws, so the transformation begins long before the image appears on paper. The process of making charcoal, transforming organic matter through fire into a material capable of producing images, becomes an integral part of the work’s conceptual and material life.

There is something particularly powerful about this process: a material associated with burning and destruction becomes the means through which new images and narratives emerge. The scale of the drawings further complicates the apparent fragility of charcoal, allowing an ephemeral and easily disturbed medium to occupy a commanding physical presence. These processes are not simply technical decisions. They are forms of knowledge produced through making. What interests me is the relationship between the resistance of materials and the artist’s desire to transform them. Materials have histories, limitations, and possibilities. They do not always behave as we expect them to. This is where the relationship with neuroplasticity becomes particularly interesting. Transformation is not necessarily about abandoning an earlier form. It can involve retaining traces of what existed before, reorganising existing structures, or discovering possibilities within apparent limitations. I also think there is a politics to these material processes. In a world increasingly preoccupied with speed, technological innovation, and instant production, the sustained labour of cutting, weaving, carving, casting, drawing, and assembling reminds us that transformation can be slow, repetitive, and demanding. It requires attention. Franklyn Dzingai, ‘ Vibrant Transmission in Musesengwe Studio ‘, 2025. Second Nature | Manyonga at La Biennale di Venezia 2026. Photo credit to Suzette Bell-Roberts.

Memory appears throughout the exhibition in different forms — personal, familial, historical and collective. Rather than treating memory as fixed, the exhibition suggests it is continually reconstructed. How do the artists approach this instability?

Memory is particularly interesting to me because we often speak about it as though it were an archive from which we retrieve intact experiences. But remembering is itself an act of reconstruction. What we remember, what we forget, and how we narrate our experiences are continually shaped by the present. The artists approach this instability through different strategies. Franklyn Dzingai’s engagement with family photographs and other visual sources raises questions about the relationship between personal recollection and collective identity. His images are not simply reproductions of remembered experiences; they are reconfigurations of them. Felix Shumba’s practice introduces another dimension through its engagement with historical violence, distortion, repetition, and speculative possibilities. His work asks what happens when historical fragments are removed from familiar narratives and made to speak differently. Gideon Gomo’s work, meanwhile, engages cultural memory through materials and sculptural traditions that carry histories of their own. What brings these approaches together is an understanding that memory is never innocent or complete. It is shaped by power, by the availability of images and narratives, and by the silences that structure our understanding of the past. I am interested in what happens when artists interrupt the apparent authority of memory. They make room for ambiguity, contradiction, and alternative interpretations. For me, this is also where the exhibition moves beyond a straightforward celebration of adaptability. If our memories are continually reconstructed, then our identities are also less stable than we might imagine. The question becomes not only how we remember, but what kinds of futures our acts of remembering make possible. Felix Shumba, ‘ Telephone Reader I- V ‘, 2025 & ‘ Telephone Reader VI- X’, 2025 & ‘ Telephone Reader Series (VBX 105; VBX 105 II; VBX 110; CYU44/antenna-dust; I-SOUND, Landscape dust) ‘, 2025. Second Nature | Manyonga at La Biennale di Venezia 2026. Photo credit to Suzette Bell-Roberts.

Several of the works move between individual experience and Zimbabwe’s wider social and historical realities. How did you negotiate that relationship without reducing the artists’ practices to a single national narrative?

This was an important consideration, particularly within the context of a national pavilion at the Venice Biennale. National pavilions carry an inherent contradiction: they bring artists together under the designation of a nation, yet artistic practices rarely conform to the boundaries or expectations of national identity. I have always been cautious about the expectation that artists from Zimbabwe must necessarily explain Zimbabwe, or that their work should be read primarily as evidence of the country’s political, economic, or social circumstances.

Of course, artists do not work outside history. Their practices emerge from particular experiences, environments, and relationships. But recognising those contexts is different from making them the sole explanation for the work. My approach was to allow the artists’ individual concerns and artistic languages to remain central. Zimbabwe is a point of connection, but it is not the limit of their intellectual or imaginative worlds. I was interested in the possibility of presenting Zimbabwean contemporary art as a field of multiple, sometimes contradictory, positions rather than a coherent national story. The exhibition’s thematic concerns with adaptation, memory, technology, and transformation are not exclusively Zimbabwean, even though the artists approach them from particular lived and historical circumstances. There is also a danger in romanticising resilience when discussing Zimbabwean artistic production.

We are frequently invited to admire how people continue to create despite difficult circumstances. While there is value in recognising that ingenuity, I think we must also question the conditions that make such ingenuity necessary. Resilience should not become a language through which structural difficulties are normalised. I wanted the Pavilion to make space for complexity, allowing the artists to be understood as producers of knowledge and imagination rather than simply representatives of a nation. Eva Raath, ‘ Absence of Memories ‘, 2025. Second Nature | Manyonga at La Biennale di Venezia 2026. Photo credit to Suzette Bell-Roberts.

The five practices establish very different relationships with fragility, rupture and repair. Where do you see the most unexpected conversations or tensions emerging between the works once they were installed together?

One of the things I find most compelling about group exhibitions is that relationships emerge between works that may not have been anticipated during the initial curatorial process. An exhibition is never simply the sum of its individual components. The works begin to produce meanings through their proximity to one another. I am particularly interested in the tension between acts of preservation and acts of destruction, or perhaps more accurately, between what must be undone and what can be carried forward. Dzingai’s reductive printmaking, for instance, introduces the idea that something must be removed for something else to emerge. Mapondera’s transformation of discarded materials suggests another possibility, in which what has been abandoned acquires new significance. These practices offer different understandings of loss and renewal. Gomo’s engagement with sculptural traditions raises questions about inheritance and reinvention, while Shumba’s reworking of historical fragments introduces a more unsettling understanding of transformation. Raath’s sustained attention to patterns and visual languages offers yet another way of considering how forms travel, persist, and change.

What emerges between these practices is a productive disagreement about the nature of repair. Can everything be repaired? Does transformation necessarily involve healing? Are there histories or experiences that resist being made whole again? I think these questions are important because contemporary discourse sometimes treats repair as an inevitable or desirable conclusion. But repair can also conceal rupture, and adaptation can sometimes mean learning to live with what cannot be restored. And the ability to transform is not the same as the freedom to determine the conditions of one’s transformation. The exhibition interests me most when it refuses easy reconciliation. I wanted the works to hold their differences and for the viewer to encounter those differences as an invitation to think rather than a problem requiring resolution. Gideon Gomo, ‘ Grief is Just Love that Had Nowhere Else to Go ‘, 2025. Second Nature | Manyonga at La Biennale di Venezia 2026. Photo credit to Suzette Bell-Roberts.

If ‘Second Nature | Manyonga’ is concerned with our capacity to change in response to experience, what do you hope remains unsettled, altered or newly visible for the viewer after encountering the exhibition?

I hope visitors leave with a more complicated understanding of transformation, particularly the idea that our capacity to adapt is neither limitless nor necessarily liberating. We live in a moment when change is frequently presented as an unquestionable good. We are expected to adapt to new technologies, shifting economic conditions, political uncertainties, and increasingly precarious ways of living. Adaptability has almost become a moral obligation. But I think we need to ask who is being asked to adapt, to what circumstances, and at what cost. One of the questions at the heart of ‘Second Nature | Manyonga ’ is what happens to our understanding of the human when the boundaries between the biological, technological, material, and social become increasingly unstable. The exhibition’s engagement with neuroplasticity opens up the possibility that we are continually becoming, but it also asks us to consider what shapes that becoming.

I would like viewers to recognise that transformation does not always announce itself through spectacular change. Sometimes it happens through small gestures, through the patient reworking of materials, through remembering differently, or through refusing inherited ways of understanding the world. And perhaps I would like them to leave with a certain discomfort about the language of resilience. We celebrate the ability to bend without breaking, but we rarely ask why so much bending is required in the first place. For me, art offers a space in which these questions can remain open. It does not necessarily provide solutions, but it can interrupt what we have come to regard as natural, inevitable, or unchangeable. If there is one thing I hope remains with the viewer, it is the recognition that what we call second nature is not necessarily permanent, and what appears inevitable might still be imagined otherwise. Pardon Mapondera, ‘ Ngwarai Vanangu ‘, 2026. Second Nature | Manyonga at La Biennale di Venezia 2026. Photo credit to Suzette Bell-Roberts.
