article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "In celebration of Criterion’s The Complete Kubrick , we’re publishing a season of features dedicated to the filmmaker’s oeuvre and beyond, going through Criterion’s box set era by era and disc by disc—plus a couple of surprises from the archives. Explore more here and read part two below.", "links": [{"text": "The Complete Kubrick", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/he-wanted-the-films-to-survive-michael-chaiken-on-assembling-the-complete-kubrick/"}, {"text": "here", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/the-complete-kubrick-a-season-of-celebrating-the-legendary-director/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Killing (1956)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Killing_image_01-1200x722.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Kubrick’s first studio film is also his first unqualified artistic success: a swift, lean and biting noir that (despite a few key low-angle closeups and ominous tracking shots) trades the grandiose visual and musical experimentation most commonly identified as “Kubrickian” for equally groundbreaking experimentation with narrative structure."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Dissecting the perfect crime, the nonlinear, multi-perspective ensemble heist film follows a conspiracy of workaday men and women, led by future Jack D. Ripper Sterling Hayden as a cocky ex-con methodically plotting his masterpiece, in a complex and audacious scheme to rob a Chicago racetrack mid-race. Based on the pulp novel Clean Break by Lionel White and utilizing the jagged, crunchy mock-stained-glass prose of Kubrick’s favorite hardboiled writer Jim Thompson to bring the scheming dialogues to life, each of the film’s stock viewpoint characters is the protagonist of their own story: Jay C. Flippen as the heist’s cautious bankroller, revealed late in the film to be motivated by concern for his sickly wife; Elisha Cook Jr. as the diminutive teller, desperate to prove his masculinity; Marie Windsor as his unsatisfied wife, a sassy fork-tongued manipulator with designs of her own; Timothy Carey as the hissing, strutting, puppy-loving sniper who never misses his mark; Kola Kwariani as the Russian chessmaster, dissident intellectual and wrestler who, in a perfect Kubrickian irony, is hired as the dumb muscle of the operation."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Rather than dwell on or empathize with any one player, Kubrick’s relentlessly-paced film instead likens them to racehorses, chess pieces and puzzle pieces, continually shuffling perspectives as the clock jumps forward and backward, restaging the same scenes from overlapping viewpoints as the baroque grand design gradually comes into view for the audience. Each piece is maneuvered into the correct place at the correct time to outwit and burgle the inflexible system of state-condoned racetrack security. This player is to execute the feint here, so that one can penetrate the system’s defenses there, so the next one can receive the handoff during the designated window at the designated spot and move on before the mark knows what hit ‘em. The tropes of the heist movie, already established in John Huston’s 1950 The Asphalt Jungle , are combined with Kubrick’s distinct passions for chess, philosophy and tragicomic absurdism to crackerjack effect: each individual fancies themselves the master strategist of their world, but is only privy to a limited piece of the bigger picture. Even the perfect scheme struggles to survive contact with the frailties of the human heart—lust, hatred, and one-sided love—combined with the vicissitudes of chance in a world of individuals one has never even met."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One of his less-seen films today, Kubrick’s breakout hit has nevertheless proven as seminal to generations of American crime cinema as his later masterpieces would be to science fiction, horror and war films. Without the chilly ironies and subversive chronology of The Killing , the outputs of David Mamet, Quentin Tarantino, the Coen brothers, Paul Thomas Anderson, Christopher Nolan, and Rian Johnson—to name a few—would be unrecognizable. Amusingly though, for his trouble constructing a bleeding-cool auteurist pulp pastiche that reveals the small-minded artifice of traditional Hollywood forms by scrambling their structure, Kubrick was initially written off as a poseur by Cahiers du cinéma critic Jean-Luc Godard. A more senior film artist, on the other hand, had a different view: The Killing inspired one Orson Welles to promptly declare Kubrick the greatest director of his generation. Given his own output, it’s not hard to imagine what enchanted Welles: The Killing isn’t just a successful Hollywood entertainment, but a winking piece of metacinema that not-too-subtly likens the film director to the criminal mastermind, playfully hoodwinking the audience with the unique power over comprehension and perception exercised behind the camera before humbly submitting to the impossibility of total control."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Paths of Glory (1957)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/PathsOfGlory_image_08-1200x726.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "If The Killing cemented Kubrick as a young maverick in exceptional command of cinematic storytelling, Paths of Glory announced him as a serious artist with serious thoughts on his mind. Adapting WWI veteran Humphrey Cobb’s novel of the same name, Kubrick reunited with Jim Thompson alongside playwright Calder Willingham (also a one-time collaborator of David Lean, Mike Nichols, Arthur Penn, Marlon Brando, and Jack Garfein ) to craft one of the great war film screenplays, a figurative slow pan up and down the ranks of the 1916 French armed forces in a Sisyphean 90-minute chronicle of institutional friendly fire.", "links": [{"text": "Jack Garfein", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/psychic-scars-and-something-wild-a-conversation-with-dramatist-filmmaker-and-holocaust-survivor-jack-garfein/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There are quite a few literal slow pans and tracking shots too, of course, and Kubrick combines them with masterful blocking to establish the film’s two conflicting settings and worlds. There’s the palatial French estate (the same used in Last Year at Marienbad ), established with ornate period architecture, angular military formations, and graceful X and Y-axis camera movements, where well-mustached generals (real-life WWI vet Adolphe Menjou and subordinate George Macready) dine on fine food, enjoy waltzes, and relay a casualty-heavy, practically infeasible strategy to repel Germany’s forces from above—no one wants to be deemed a coward and relieved of his command, so responsibility for the foolhardy assault is kicked continually down the ranks. And then there’s the snaking, filthy, crowded trenches, represented in claustrophobic lateral tracking shots, where the infantrymen treated as livestock and game pieces have to live with the shelling, the sickness, the dwindling rations, the omnipresence of terror and death, and the condescension of generals touring the frontlines to deny the existence of “shellshock” and demand to know whether each and every soldier is “Ready to kill more Germans?”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Serving as liaison between these conflicting strata is Kirk Douglas, the lone uncomplicatedly heroic leading man in the Kubrick corpus, as stout-hearted patriot Col. Dax, charged with the contradictory duties of protecting his men and obeying his callous superiors. In a subversion of genre norms, the film’s big battle sequence—the charge on the heavily fortified “Anthill,” filmed in slow, grueling right-to-left horizontal movements through fields of fire and flying dirt—is not the climax of the film, but its midpoint. When the operation fails just as Dax warned it would—due in part to the actual cowardice of nepo-officer Lt. Roget (Wayne Morris)—three corpsmen (Ralph Meeker alongside the returning Timothy Carey and Joe Turkel) are chosen as scapegoats to answer for the strategic and moral failures of their promotion-hungry superiors, men who disguise their interest in advancing and maintaining their own dominance as the interest of the state. The final act and climax are a grimly absurd show trial, imprisonment and execution, redolent of Camus’ The Stranger and shot in the film’s most imposing expressionist compositions, in which Dax’s shrewd dissections of the accusers’ obscene logic and the innocent prisoners’ own heartrending, “cowardly” pleas for their lives fall on deaf ears. “There are few things more fundamentally encouraging and stimulating than seeing someone else die!” beams Menjou’s cheerful, wine-sipping Maj. General Broulard while condemning his own countrymen—including, by the end, a man with a concussion who needs to be propped up and prodded awake for his own execution—to senseless deaths as communal spectacle, “for morale.” Broulard is a man, like the film’s other men of power, whose cold strategic models and macho death-cult ideals cannot countenance or survive flesh-and-blood human frailty, and whose hierarchical insulation from consequences for his own frailty diminishes his humanity."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Paths of Glory was an intellectually, professionally, and personally monumental film for Kubrick, held back only by his Hays Code-enforced inability to graphically depict war’s desecration of the body in ways he instead leans on (dreadfully evocative) dialogue to describe. (There is one gruesome exception: the image of a smoldering soldier killed by his own lieutenant’s hand grenade, thrown on an ill-advised nighttime mission in a fit of panic. His killer never faces any consequences.) For its harsh portrayal of the French military in a defensive war against Germany, with WWII so close in the rearview mirror, the film was deemed scandalous in France and denied distribution for nearly two decades. Of course Kubrick’s point was not to attack France: he treats them no less kindly than he would treat America in Dr. Strangelove and Full Metal Jacket , and presumably kinder than he would have treated Nazi Germany in the unrealized Holocaust film he was already contemplating by the late 1950s (an early concept of which—to follow the domestic life of a Nazi officer involved in the extermination of European Jewry—bears a notable resemblance to Jonathan Glazer’s The Zone of Interest ). Rather, Kubrick’s aim was to demonstrate the hypocrisies of hierarchical power and the logic of the nation-state as universal evils."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Extending the absurdist themes of The Killing , Paths of Glory brings the conflict of individuals and systems into sharper political focus. The film foreshadows much of Kubrick’s future work with its forensic depiction of individual men’s egocentric and rationally self-interested maneuvers within a state institution producing, in concert, abjectly cruel and irrational outcomes, devouring the weak while destroying the strong from within. Kubrick’s most humanist film also illustrates his evolving ideas about human nature: here war reduces men to numbers and thus to lesser, colder versions of themselves, compelling them to assume masks of detachment and barbarism as they’re told their natural desire to live is cowardice and their natural individuality is illusory before the uniform abstraction of the nation. (Kubrick’s clever casting and framing emphasize the men’s individuality in size, shape, and skin tone even as they stand shoulder to shoulder in uniform.) One of the film’s most repellent antagonists, Macready’s Brig. Gen. Mireau, initially seems sympathetic and protective of his division until his command is threatened from above; Kubrick’s Rousseauist ideas about cruelty as learned behavior would be complicated by later films that weigh the dehumanizing effect of social systems of control against the violent and senseless aspects of man’s barbarian and animal heritage. The grimly ironic, procedurally detailed depiction of a self-cannibalizing institution in which “the shit rolls downhill” would also be a key inspiration for revered TV writer David Simon, who has cited it as a template for the 21st-century stories of HBO’s The Wire and Generation Kill ."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Paths of Glory was also, finally, the film that introduced Stanley to actress Christiane Harlan, his third wife and the love of his life—and, in an irony Kubrick himself couldn’t have bettered, the niece of infamous Nazi filmmaker Veit Harlan, director of likely the most antisemitic film ever made, the Holocaust-era agitprop drama Süss the Jew . To Kubrick, one of the great Jewish filmmakers whose awareness of his own Jewishness and haunted fascination with the Holocaust would only grow as the years went by, the notion of guilt by association hardly registered. With Christiane (and her brother Jan, eventually to be a trusted production partner and guardian of the Kubrick estate), Kubrick would be personally and artistically transformed, raising three daughters as he matured from young upstart to wise master, and remained blissfully married until his death more than four decades later. In Paths of Glory ’s coda, she plays the lone female character in the entire film: a tearful German girl coerced by the French troops, brought to a drunken tavern to sing before a crowd of leering, barking, animalistic men ready to let loose the pent-up cruelty of the trenches. As her halting nightingale voice rises in the German folksong “The Faithful Hussar”, the masks of barbarism slip from the men in a montage of faces steadily joining her in singing and in tears. For just a fleeting moment before their redeployment, the power of music and visage of a woman acts on them like the opposite of a gun: it destroys rather than reinforces the boundaries of nations, and sheds away everything that death and war have made of men. It’s the most personal and heartfelt grace note imaginable for the likes of Stanley Kubrick.", "links": [{"text": "Süss the Jew", "url": "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jud_S%C3%BC%C3%9F"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Criterion’s 4K Paths of Glory disc features a commentary reused from their 2010 Blu-ray, in which critic and author Gary Giddins offers an exhaustive breakdown of the film’s innovative technique, cast and production history, subtle symbolism, revealing changes from the novel, and comparisons to other war films—most of which, unsurprisingly, reveal just how exceptional Kubrick’s directing is even when quietly supporting an exemplary script and set of performances. Arguing against the popular characterization of Paths of Glory as an “antiwar film,” Giddins dissects the verbal chess matches between characters, along with the various ways in which they’re shot, scored, and performed, to highlight how Kubrick uses the theme of war as a platform to examine issues of power, control, and class. Despite some factual errors (Giddins repeatedly misidentifies the waltz favored by Maj. Gen. Broulard as “The Blue Danube” of 2001: A Space Odyssey fame; in fact, it is “Künstlerleben,” also by Johann Strauss), the commentary is a must for those eager to discover whole new layers in a deceptively complex film."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Spartacus (1960)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Spartacus_image_07-1200x541.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For his Roman sword-and-sandal epic, Kubrick took over directing duties from postwar genre pioneer Anthony Mann—after filming had already begun—at the invitation of executive producer and star Kirk Douglas. The finished film is the one “studio picture” over which Kubrick felt little sense of authorship, though a Kubrick-approved 1991 reconstruction (the basis for Criterion’s disc) restored several provocative scenes and shots cut by Universal from the original release. It’s nevertheless Douglas and HUAC-persecuted screenwriter Dalton Trumbo’s film at heart, with Kubrick as uncharacteristic journeyman merely translating their words and characters to the cinematic canvas."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adapting the historical novel by Howard Fast, Spartacus is a thunderous, speechifying, and comparatively left-wing peer to the likes of Ben-Hur and The Ten Commandments , ditching its contemporaries’ Christianity for an insistently secular parable of the ancient world, framed around the eternal struggle of social underclasses against the wages of exploitation and imperialism. While loosely based on the actual life of the man Karl Marx deemed “the most splendid fellow in all of ancient history,” the film’s vision of Rome—shared by Fast, Trumbo and Kubrick despite a host of other creative differences—analogizes the cruel and decadent twilight years of the Republic clearly enough to a postwar America riven by inequality that it inspired backlash in its day, with prominent conservatives including John Wayne calling for boycotts of the blacklist-breaking production."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Spartacus (Douglas) is a Thracian born into the crucible of slavery, whose muscular stature and knack for defiance earn him a spot in the lucrative and deadly gladiatorial circuit under oily manager Lentulus Batiatus (snake charmer Peter Ustinov, who wrote a substantial portion of his own dialogue to create an urbane and affable antagonist where lesser actors might have leaned into one-note vulgarity). Forced to fight his fellow slaves for the entertainment of Rome’s upper classes—“ladies and gentlemen of quality, those who appreciate a fine kill,” as Batiatus puts it—Spartacus is eventually spurred from quiet defiance to collective solidarity and open rebellion by the petty cruelty of power-hungry oligarch Marcus Licinius Crassus (Laurence Olivier, who like Ustinov sketches welcome texture into what could have been a cutout villain—as in a memorable scene, cut by studio censors from the original 1960 release, in which the surprisingly libertine Crassus reveals himself through salacious culinary double entendre as one of Hollywood’s first openly bisexual characters). Crassus in turn finds himself opposed both on the battlefield by Spartacus and in the chambers of the Senate by corpulent operator Sempronius Gracchus (Charles Laughton), a principled sleaze who correctly perceives Crassus’ ever-growing authority as foreshadowing the collapse of the Republic into an Empire."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As the black sheep of the Kubrick oeuvre, Spartacus is distinct for its stylistic indistinctness amid the genre blockbusters of its day. It’s Stanley’s most talkative film by a mile, filled to the over-three-hour brim with moralistic and expository speechifying, filmed in mostly conventional shot-reverse shot coverage to highlight the performances of its hallowed thespians. It’s also the only Kubrick film with no ambiguity or irony of note: a clash of noble heroes and dastardly villains all neatly sorted out from one another by the pyrrhic finale, with bellowed Trumbo monologues telling the audience what to think and an insistent full-orchestra Alex North score telling them what to feel at all times, should any questions arise. Yet it’s not without distinct traces of Kubrick: dense and wordless panoramic shots establish the scope, depth, and brutality of the film’s world in between dialogue scenes, with clear distinctions drawn between the loose, rough and warm compositions of Spartacus’s growing slave army—in which women, children, and the elderly march to the sea alongside barely-trained men—and the cool, angular regimentation of “civilized” Rome. A morbid vertical tracking shot of corpses stacked to the blood-red horizon in the aftermath of battle is one of the great moving images in the Kubrick library. Institutional decay and barbarism in the guise of civilization return as central Kubrickian themes, and the director clearly takes special interest in aspects of the script exploring the psychosexual and gendered dimensions of power, dehumanization and control: the first act draws particular attention to the commodification of Spartacus’s masculine body and persona by the thirsty consumers of the Roman slaveholding class."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It’s also an early instance of a Kubrick film presenting indirect, secularized reimaginings of distinctly Jewish narratives: the Roman-Judean conflict is never brought up in the film, yet the framing of the ostensibly pagan Spartacus as armed anti-Roman rebel and unassuming liberator-prophet evokes martyred Hebrew anti-occupation militants like the Sicarii and the slave exodus of Moses. Crucially though, Spartacus is not motivated by religious, ethnic or ideological agendas but by his material conditions and thoroughly individual human desires: the final spark that sets off his revolution is not an intellectualized call to arms but his erotically evoked and consensually reciprocated love for the female slave Varinia (Jean Simmons), whose defiant spirit in spite of her bodily captivity raises the acquisitive lust and ire of Crassus."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "To Kubrick, the value of Spartacus was mainly pragmatic: its success assured him the clout to secure studio backing for his more personally ambitious future projects. And a success it was: the film’s box office returns dwarfed Kubrick’s combined previous efforts by orders of magnitude, winning four Academy Awards (albeit none personally for Kubrick) and such high-profile fans as newly elected President John F. article_text:
In celebration of Criterion’s The Complete Kubrick , we’re publishing a season of features dedicated to the filmmaker’s oeuvre and beyond, going through Criterion’s box set era by era and disc by disc—plus a couple of surprises from the archives. Explore more here and read part two below.

The Killing (1956)

Kubrick’s first studio film is also his first unqualified artistic success: a swift, lean and biting noir that (despite a few key low-angle closeups and ominous tracking shots) trades the grandiose visual and musical experimentation most commonly identified as “Kubrickian” for equally groundbreaking experimentation with narrative structure.

Dissecting the perfect crime, the nonlinear, multi-perspective ensemble heist film follows a conspiracy of workaday men and women, led by future Jack D. Ripper Sterling Hayden as a cocky ex-con methodically plotting his masterpiece, in a complex and audacious scheme to rob a Chicago racetrack mid-race. Based on the pulp novel Clean Break by Lionel White and utilizing the jagged, crunchy mock-stained-glass prose of Kubrick’s favorite hardboiled writer Jim Thompson to bring the scheming dialogues to life, each of the film’s stock viewpoint characters is the protagonist of their own story: Jay C. Flippen as the heist’s cautious bankroller, revealed late in the film to be motivated by concern for his sickly wife; Elisha Cook Jr. as the diminutive teller, desperate to prove his masculinity; Marie Windsor as his unsatisfied wife, a sassy fork-tongued manipulator with designs of her own; Timothy Carey as the hissing, strutting, puppy-loving sniper who never misses his mark; Kola Kwariani as the Russian chessmaster, dissident intellectual and wrestler who, in a perfect Kubrickian irony, is hired as the dumb muscle of the operation.

Rather than dwell on or empathize with any one player, Kubrick’s relentlessly-paced film instead likens them to racehorses, chess pieces and puzzle pieces, continually shuffling perspectives as the clock jumps forward and backward, restaging the same scenes from overlapping viewpoints as the baroque grand design gradually comes into view for the audience. Each piece is maneuvered into the correct place at the correct time to outwit and burgle the inflexible system of state-condoned racetrack security. This player is to execute the feint here, so that one can penetrate the system’s defenses there, so the next one can receive the handoff during the designated window at the designated spot and move on before the mark knows what hit ‘em. The tropes of the heist movie, already established in John Huston’s 1950 The Asphalt Jungle , are combined with Kubrick’s distinct passions for chess, philosophy and tragicomic absurdism to crackerjack effect: each individual fancies themselves the master strategist of their world, but is only privy to a limited piece of the bigger picture. Even the perfect scheme struggles to survive contact with the frailties of the human heart—lust, hatred, and one-sided love—combined with the vicissitudes of chance in a world of individuals one has never even met.

One of his less-seen films today, Kubrick’s breakout hit has nevertheless proven as seminal to generations of American crime cinema as his later masterpieces would be to science fiction, horror and war films. Without the chilly ironies and subversive chronology of The Killing , the outputs of David Mamet, Quentin Tarantino, the Coen brothers, Paul Thomas Anderson, Christopher Nolan, and Rian Johnson—to name a few—would be unrecognizable. Amusingly though, for his trouble constructing a bleeding-cool auteurist pulp pastiche that reveals the small-minded artifice of traditional Hollywood forms by scrambling their structure, Kubrick was initially written off as a poseur by Cahiers du cinéma critic Jean-Luc Godard. A more senior film artist, on the other hand, had a different view: The Killing inspired one Orson Welles to promptly declare Kubrick the greatest director of his generation. Given his own output, it’s not hard to imagine what enchanted Welles: The Killing isn’t just a successful Hollywood entertainment, but a winking piece of metacinema that not-too-subtly likens the film director to the criminal mastermind, playfully hoodwinking the audience with the unique power over comprehension and perception exercised behind the camera before humbly submitting to the impossibility of total control.

Paths of Glory (1957)

If The Killing cemented Kubrick as a young maverick in exceptional command of cinematic storytelling, Paths of Glory announced him as a serious artist with serious thoughts on his mind. Adapting WWI veteran Humphrey Cobb’s novel of the same name, Kubrick reunited with Jim Thompson alongside playwright Calder Willingham (also a one-time collaborator of David Lean, Mike Nichols, Arthur Penn, Marlon Brando, and Jack Garfein ) to craft one of the great war film screenplays, a figurative slow pan up and down the ranks of the 1916 French armed forces in a Sisyphean 90-minute chronicle of institutional friendly fire.

There are quite a few literal slow pans and tracking shots too, of course, and Kubrick combines them with masterful blocking to establish the film’s two conflicting settings and worlds. There’s the palatial French estate (the same used in Last Year at Marienbad ), established with ornate period architecture, angular military formations, and graceful X and Y-axis camera movements, where well-mustached generals (real-life WWI vet Adolphe Menjou and subordinate George Macready) dine on fine food, enjoy waltzes, and relay a casualty-heavy, practically infeasible strategy to repel Germany’s forces from above—no one wants to be deemed a coward and relieved of his command, so responsibility for the foolhardy assault is kicked continually down the ranks. And then there’s the snaking, filthy, crowded trenches, represented in claustrophobic lateral tracking shots, where the infantrymen treated as livestock and game pieces have to live with the shelling, the sickness, the dwindling rations, the omnipresence of terror and death, and the condescension of generals touring the frontlines to deny the existence of “shellshock” and demand to know whether each and every soldier is “Ready to kill more Germans?”

Serving as liaison between these conflicting strata is Kirk Douglas, the lone uncomplicatedly heroic leading man in the Kubrick corpus, as stout-hearted patriot Col. Dax, charged with the contradictory duties of protecting his men and obeying his callous superiors. In a subversion of genre norms, the film’s big battle sequence—the charge on the heavily fortified “Anthill,” filmed in slow, grueling right-to-left horizontal movements through fields of fire and flying dirt—is not the climax of the film, but its midpoint. When the operation fails just as Dax warned it would—due in part to the actual cowardice of nepo-officer Lt. Roget (Wayne Morris)—three corpsmen (Ralph Meeker alongside the returning Timothy Carey and Joe Turkel) are chosen as scapegoats to answer for the strategic and moral failures of their promotion-hungry superiors, men who disguise their interest in advancing and maintaining their own dominance as the interest of the state. The final act and climax are a grimly absurd show trial, imprisonment and execution, redolent of Camus’ The Stranger and shot in the film’s most imposing expressionist compositions, in which Dax’s shrewd dissections of the accusers’ obscene logic and the innocent prisoners’ own heartrending, “cowardly” pleas for their lives fall on deaf ears. “There are few things more fundamentally encouraging and stimulating than seeing someone else die!” beams Menjou’s cheerful, wine-sipping Maj. General Broulard while condemning his own countrymen—including, by the end, a man with a concussion who needs to be propped up and prodded awake for his own execution—to senseless deaths as communal spectacle, “for morale.” Broulard is a man, like the film’s other men of power, whose cold strategic models and macho death-cult ideals cannot countenance or survive flesh-and-blood human frailty, and whose hierarchical insulation from consequences for his own frailty diminishes his humanity.

Paths of Glory was an intellectually, professionally, and personally monumental film for Kubrick, held back only by his Hays Code-enforced inability to graphically depict war’s desecration of the body in ways he instead leans on (dreadfully evocative) dialogue to describe. (There is one gruesome exception: the image of a smoldering soldier killed by his own lieutenant’s hand grenade, thrown on an ill-advised nighttime mission in a fit of panic. His killer never faces any consequences.) For its harsh portrayal of the French military in a defensive war against Germany, with WWII so close in the rearview mirror, the film was deemed scandalous in France and denied distribution for nearly two decades. Of course Kubrick’s point was not to attack France: he treats them no less kindly than he would treat America in Dr. Strangelove and Full Metal Jacket , and presumably kinder than he would have treated Nazi Germany in the unrealized Holocaust film he was already contemplating by the late 1950s (an early concept of which—to follow the domestic life of a Nazi officer involved in the extermination of European Jewry—bears a notable resemblance to Jonathan Glazer’s The Zone of Interest ). Rather, Kubrick’s aim was to demonstrate the hypocrisies of hierarchical power and the logic of the nation-state as universal evils.

Extending the absurdist themes of The Killing , Paths of Glory brings the conflict of individuals and systems into sharper political focus. The film foreshadows much of Kubrick’s future work with its forensic depiction of individual men’s egocentric and rationally self-interested maneuvers within a state institution producing, in concert, abjectly cruel and irrational outcomes, devouring the weak while destroying the strong from within. Kubrick’s most humanist film also illustrates his evolving ideas about human nature: here war reduces men to numbers and thus to lesser, colder versions of themselves, compelling them to assume masks of detachment and barbarism as they’re told their natural desire to live is cowardice and their natural individuality is illusory before the uniform abstraction of the nation. (Kubrick’s clever casting and framing emphasize the men’s individuality in size, shape, and skin tone even as they stand shoulder to shoulder in uniform.) One of the film’s most repellent antagonists, Macready’s Brig. Gen. Mireau, initially seems sympathetic and protective of his division until his command is threatened from above; Kubrick’s Rousseauist ideas about cruelty as learned behavior would be complicated by later films that weigh the dehumanizing effect of social systems of control against the violent and senseless aspects of man’s barbarian and animal heritage. The grimly ironic, procedurally detailed depiction of a self-cannibalizing institution in which “the shit rolls downhill” would also be a key inspiration for revered TV writer David Simon, who has cited it as a template for the 21st-century stories of HBO’s The Wire and Generation Kill .

Paths of Glory was also, finally, the film that introduced Stanley to actress Christiane Harlan, his third wife and the love of his life—and, in an irony Kubrick himself couldn’t have bettered, the niece of infamous Nazi filmmaker Veit Harlan, director of likely the most antisemitic film ever made, the Holocaust-era agitprop drama Süss the Jew . To Kubrick, one of the great Jewish filmmakers whose awareness of his own Jewishness and haunted fascination with the Holocaust would only grow as the years went by, the notion of guilt by association hardly registered. With Christiane (and her brother Jan, eventually to be a trusted production partner and guardian of the Kubrick estate), Kubrick would be personally and artistically transformed, raising three daughters as he matured from young upstart to wise master, and remained blissfully married until his death more than four decades later. In Paths of Glory ’s coda, she plays the lone female character in the entire film: a tearful German girl coerced by the French troops, brought to a drunken tavern to sing before a crowd of leering, barking, animalistic men ready to let loose the pent-up cruelty of the trenches. As her halting nightingale voice rises in the German folksong “The Faithful Hussar”, the masks of barbarism slip from the men in a montage of faces steadily joining her in singing and in tears. For just a fleeting moment before their redeployment, the power of music and visage of a woman acts on them like the opposite of a gun: it destroys rather than reinforces the boundaries of nations, and sheds away everything that death and war have made of men. It’s the most personal and heartfelt grace note imaginable for the likes of Stanley Kubrick.

Criterion’s 4K Paths of Glory disc features a commentary reused from their 2010 Blu-ray, in which critic and author Gary Giddins offers an exhaustive breakdown of the film’s innovative technique, cast and production history, subtle symbolism, revealing changes from the novel, and comparisons to other war films—most of which, unsurprisingly, reveal just how exceptional Kubrick’s directing is even when quietly supporting an exemplary script and set of performances. Arguing against the popular characterization of Paths of Glory as an “antiwar film,” Giddins dissects the verbal chess matches between characters, along with the various ways in which they’re shot, scored, and performed, to highlight how Kubrick uses the theme of war as a platform to examine issues of power, control, and class. Despite some factual errors (Giddins repeatedly misidentifies the waltz favored by Maj. Gen. Broulard as “The Blue Danube” of 2001: A Space Odyssey fame; in fact, it is “Künstlerleben,” also by Johann Strauss), the commentary is a must for those eager to discover whole new layers in a deceptively complex film.

Spartacus (1960)

For his Roman sword-and-sandal epic, Kubrick took over directing duties from postwar genre pioneer Anthony Mann—after filming had already begun—at the invitation of executive producer and star Kirk Douglas. The finished film is the one “studio picture” over which Kubrick felt little sense of authorship, though a Kubrick-approved 1991 reconstruction (the basis for Criterion’s disc) restored several provocative scenes and shots cut by Universal from the original release. It’s nevertheless Douglas and HUAC-persecuted screenwriter Dalton Trumbo’s film at heart, with Kubrick as uncharacteristic journeyman merely translating their words and characters to the cinematic canvas.

Adapting the historical novel by Howard Fast, Spartacus is a thunderous, speechifying, and comparatively left-wing peer to the likes of Ben-Hur and The Ten Commandments , ditching its contemporaries’ Christianity for an insistently secular parable of the ancient world, framed around the eternal struggle of social underclasses against the wages of exploitation and imperialism. While loosely based on the actual life of the man Karl Marx deemed “the most splendid fellow in all of ancient history,” the film’s vision of Rome—shared by Fast, Trumbo and Kubrick despite a host of other creative differences—analogizes the cruel and decadent twilight years of the Republic clearly enough to a postwar America riven by inequality that it inspired backlash in its day, with prominent conservatives including John Wayne calling for boycotts of the blacklist-breaking production.

Spartacus (Douglas) is a Thracian born into the crucible of slavery, whose muscular stature and knack for defiance earn him a spot in the lucrative and deadly gladiatorial circuit under oily manager Lentulus Batiatus (snake charmer Peter Ustinov, who wrote a substantial portion of his own dialogue to create an urbane and affable antagonist where lesser actors might have leaned into one-note vulgarity). Forced to fight his fellow slaves for the entertainment of Rome’s upper classes—“ladies and gentlemen of quality, those who appreciate a fine kill,” as Batiatus puts it—Spartacus is eventually spurred from quiet defiance to collective solidarity and open rebellion by the petty cruelty of power-hungry oligarch Marcus Licinius Crassus (Laurence Olivier, who like Ustinov sketches welcome texture into what could have been a cutout villain—as in a memorable scene, cut by studio censors from the original 1960 release, in which the surprisingly libertine Crassus reveals himself through salacious culinary double entendre as one of Hollywood’s first openly bisexual characters). Crassus in turn finds himself opposed both on the battlefield by Spartacus and in the chambers of the Senate by corpulent operator Sempronius Gracchus (Charles Laughton), a principled sleaze who correctly perceives Crassus’ ever-growing authority as foreshadowing the collapse of the Republic into an Empire.

As the black sheep of the Kubrick oeuvre, Spartacus is distinct for its stylistic indistinctness amid the genre blockbusters of its day. It’s Stanley’s most talkative film by a mile, filled to the over-three-hour brim with moralistic and expository speechifying, filmed in mostly conventional shot-reverse shot coverage to highlight the performances of its hallowed thespians. It’s also the only Kubrick film with no ambiguity or irony of note: a clash of noble heroes and dastardly villains all neatly sorted out from one another by the pyrrhic finale, with bellowed Trumbo monologues telling the audience what to think and an insistent full-orchestra Alex North score telling them what to feel at all times, should any questions arise. Yet it’s not without distinct traces of Kubrick: dense and wordless panoramic shots establish the scope, depth, and brutality of the film’s world in between dialogue scenes, with clear distinctions drawn between the loose, rough and warm compositions of Spartacus’s growing slave army—in which women, children, and the elderly march to the sea alongside barely-trained men—and the cool, angular regimentation of “civilized” Rome. A morbid vertical tracking shot of corpses stacked to the blood-red horizon in the aftermath of battle is one of the great moving images in the Kubrick library. Institutional decay and barbarism in the guise of civilization return as central Kubrickian themes, and the director clearly takes special interest in aspects of the script exploring the psychosexual and gendered dimensions of power, dehumanization and control: the first act draws particular attention to the commodification of Spartacus’s masculine body and persona by the thirsty consumers of the Roman slaveholding class.

It’s also an early instance of a Kubrick film presenting indirect, secularized reimaginings of distinctly Jewish narratives: the Roman-Judean conflict is never brought up in the film, yet the framing of the ostensibly pagan Spartacus as armed anti-Roman rebel and unassuming liberator-prophet evokes martyred Hebrew anti-occupation militants like the Sicarii and the slave exodus of Moses. Crucially though, Spartacus is not motivated by religious, ethnic or ideological agendas but by his material conditions and thoroughly individual human desires: the final spark that sets off his revolution is not an intellectualized call to arms but his erotically evoked and consensually reciprocated love for the female slave Varinia (Jean Simmons), whose defiant spirit in spite of her bodily captivity raises the acquisitive lust and ire of Crassus.

To Kubrick, the value of Spartacus was mainly pragmatic: its success assured him the clout to secure studio backing for his more personally ambitious future projects. And a success it was: the film’s box office returns dwarfed Kubrick’s combined previous efforts by orders of magnitude, winning four Academy Awards (albeit none personally for Kubrick) and such high-profile fans as newly elected President John F. Kennedy. The film’s most iconic scene and line—“ I am Spartacus! ”, an inclusion initially resisted by Kubrick for being too corny—became a cultural meme that survives to this day among internet users who have, in many cases, never seen the other 196 minutes of the film. Contemporary Spartacus admirers include handpicked Kubrick disciple Steven Spielberg, who’s professed his affection for the film (to the public and to Kubrick personally) on multiple occasions; Ridley Scott, whose less ideologically charged Gladiator (and, alas, Gladiator II ) would be unimaginable without Spartacus as template; Mel Gibson, whose Braveheart is similarly indebted; and almost certainly John Milius and George Lucas, whose Conan the Barbarian and Star Wars prequel films respectively draw heavily from the images and themes of Kubrick’s epic. (One of the climactic sequences of The Phantom Menace , set in rolling green hills packed with geometrically imposing infantry and vehicle formations, is essentially the final battle of Spartacus with CGI droids and lasers—and a happier outcome.)

Criterion’s disc includes two commentary tracks, both recorded for their previous 1992 LaserDisc release. One features excerpts from Trumbo’s extensive production notes and writings on the film, read aloud by voice actors Michael McConnohie and Barbara Goodson. The other assembles an impressive array of contributors to take turns offering their perspectives on the film, including Douglas (who clearly adored it more than anyone), Ustinov (even more charming behind the mic than in front of the camera), Saul Bass (not just the film’s title designer but an art director sharing significant visual authorship with Kubrick), and Howard Fast (who in an amusing departure from commentary track norms spends much of the film’s runtime tearing it apart, nitpicking every historical inaccuracy, change from the novel and hypermasculine performance choice by Douglas in ways Kubrick himself may have agreed with). Fast at least correctly pinpoints the film’s undervalued MVP: Woody Strode (Golden Globe-nominated for only a few minutes of screen time) as the stoic Ethiopian slave Draba, whose dramatic choice to turn his spear on the masters rather than execute Spartacus for their pleasure plants the thought of revolution in the hero’s mind—and provides one of the most thrillingly intimate and gruesome scenes in the film. Its possible resonance with a 1960 American audience is left unspoken.

article_text:
Shares of Lionsgate surged more than 15% in afternoon trading Tuesday on a report the company had received a takeover offer from Legendary Entertainment, which has been kicking the tires of the stand-alone studio for months.

Deadline reported Legendary’s interest in June 2025 after Lionsgate Studios split with Starz. In a report today, Bloomberg said talks between the two had revived and Legendary, led by chief executive Josh Grode and owned by private equity giant Apollo and management, had submitted a bid.

A combination would give Legendary Pictures a theatrical distribution arm (it currently releases films with Skydance’s Paramount, with Street Fighter opening atop the box office this past weekend) as well as Lionsgate’s extensive and cash-generating library.

Watch on Deadline

Lionsgate, led by CEO Jon Feltheimer, has been a potential target for years but shares have been boosted sharply by takeover speculation amid rapid industry consolidation. After today’s runup, the stock is trading at over $12, about double its 52-week low.

Lionsgate and Legendary both declined comment.

article_text:
Deranged Minds Entertainment has announced a feature-length doc on an iconic scream queen.

Danielle Harris , the actress who was in four “ Halloween ” films and many more projects, is the subject of a new film about her life and career shot over the last three years.

Per the official description, “Before she was old enough to drive, Danielle Harris had outrun Michael Myers twice and held her own opposite Bruce Willis and Roseanne Barr. Off screen, she survived far worse: her father’s death in an unsolved car accident, the suicides of a famous partner and a close friend, a stalker who tracked her for two decades and a pregnancy complication that stopped her heart.”

Related Stories

Cynthia Erivo Imagines Competing on 'The Great British Bake Off' in 'SNL U.K.' Opening Monologue: 'I've Got a Soggy Bottom and I'm Freaking Stressed!'

Cynthia Erivo's 'Bad Fairies' Adds Kylie Minogue, Jonathan Groff and Catherine Tate to Voice Cast

The documentary includes archival footage, private home video and interviews with Harris, her family, friends and collaborators.

“People think they know Danielle because they grew up watching her,” director and producer Destinie Orndoff said in a statement. “They’ve seen the performances. They’ve never seen what it cost her, and Danielle didn’t hold anything back.”

Some of Harris’ film credits include 1988’s “Halloween 4: The Return of Michael Myers,” 1989’s “Halloween 5: The Revenge of Michael Myers,” 1991’s “Don’t Tell Mom the Babysitter’s Dead,” 2007’s “Halloween” and 2009’s “Halloween II.” She also appeared on TV in shows like “Roseanne” and “The Wild Thornberrys.”

“In the three years of filming, I had the honor of getting to know the woman off the screen,” director and producer Tristan Clay said in a statement. “I can’t wait for audiences to see this side of her.”

The documentary is currently in post-production, with a festival run planned for 2027. It is produced by Orndoff, Clay, Hayden Todd Wilberger and Jordan Wyant. Distribution inquiries can be sent to derangedmindsentertainment@yahoo.com.

Watch a trailer for the documentary below.

article_text:
Audiences can’t get enough of Elizabeth Holmes.

Eight years after Theranos, her blood-testing startup collapsed in spectacular fashion, “ You Can See Everything ,” a gonzo documentary about Holmes, opened to a staggering $15 million from 855 screens. That ranks as the second-best opening for a non-music documentary in history, just behind 2004’s “Fahrenheit 9/11,” which debuted to $23.9 million. Remember, however, that Michael Moore’s takedown of Bushism was released in the hothouse atmosphere of an election year. “You Can See Everything” comes after Holmes has been everywhere for nearly a decade, popping up in podcasts, in documentaries from the likes of Alex Gibney, in best-sellers, and on TV, where she was memorably portrayed by Amanda Seyfried.

Yet A24 was able to maintain interest in the convicted fraudster, teasing out the secrets that Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim ‘s documentary promised to disclose without ever revealing its surprises. Audiences intent on not having the whole thing spoiled snapped up tickets, with A24 reporting that there were more than 2,000 sellouts.

The film ‘s success is a testament to a clever marketing campaign that by revealing next to nothing, somehow made “You Can See Everything” even more of an event . It’s also a credit to Nathan Fielder, the film’s co-director, who has cultivated a strong following through shows like Comedy Central’s “Nathan for You” and HBO’s “The Rehearsal,” that push meta to the breaking point. His awkward energy seemed perfectly matched for whatever Holmes is serving up through those unblinking eyes. Fielder’s co-director, Lance Oppenheim, is also riding high, having recently directed another A24 hit , the Robert Pattinson drama “Primetime.” That look at “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen has grossed nearly $45 million on a $14.5 million budget. “You Can See Everything” carries a $7 million budget, setting itself up for a very, very profitable run.

Last year at this time, A24 was in rough shape . It had raised $75 million in 2024 from Thrive Capital which valued the company at a massive $3.5 billion. Then it used that money to invest in some real duds, including “The Smashing Machine,” which cost $50 million and was supposed to score Dwayne Johnson an Oscar until it sunk like a rock at the box office , grossing a measly $21.1 million. Other costly flops included Ari Aster “Eddington,” which offered a return to the COVID era that audiences roundly rejected.

But since “Marty Supreme” opened in December of 2025, A24 has been on an epic hot streak. The drama about a ping-pong player became A24’s highest-grossing release ever, earning $192.4 million on a $70 million budget. But that record didn’t last long. “Backrooms” premiered in the summer, grossing more than $400 million on a $10 million budget. There have still been flops (justice for “Mother Mary”), but A24 hits like “Tony” and “The Drama” have outnumbered its misses. With major studios like Warner Bros. and Fox getting sold off or disappearing, A24 and its $3.5 billion valuation stand out like a beacon of hope to auteurs like Fielder and Oppenheim, promising them both artistic freedom and a chance to reach a wider audience than they otherwise might have dreamed of attracting.

Of course, it helps to have a killer marketing hook. In Holmes, an erstwhile entrepreneur who hoodwinked Beltway power brokers and captains of industry before lighting billions of dollars on fire, “You Can See Everything” demonstrates once again that nothing is as fascinating as a fall from grace.
excerpt_original: Audiences rushed to theaters as Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's Elizabeth Holmes documentary arrived shrouded in secrecy.

article_text:
Industrial Light & Magic animation supervisor Hal Hickel approached Jon Favreau ’s “ The Mandalorian and Grogu ” with a deceptively simple question: “What would Phil do?”

The Phil in question was stop-motion pioneer Phil Tippett , whose work on the original “ Star Wars ” trilogy provided a template for everything from lumbering AT-AT walkers to a spectacular battle involving two giant droids animated by hand.

Speaking at View Conference in Turin on Thursday, Hickel, who recently marked 30 years at ILM, detailed how the team mixed digital animation with physical sets, mechanical rigs and traditional stop-motion. He also recounted returning to Tippett’s Berkeley stage to animate a shot himself.

For the movie’s opening AT-AT battle , Hickel revived animation tests developed for “Rogue One,” which had involved inserting computer-generated walkers into footage from the original trilogy to study its lighting, textures and stop-motion feel. The new walkers moved even more slowly to emphasize their enormous weight. A full-sized interior set extended through a walker’s neck into its movable head, while a planned exchange of gunfire between characters riding on two walkers was filmed but ultimately cut.

The smaller AT-RT presented a different challenge. Animators studied ostriches before feeding their digital movement curves into a six-axis mechanical rig carrying the performers. Initial tests shook the contraption so violently that Hickel joked, “Poor Grogu. He was not going to survive.” Favreau wanted the vehicle bouncy, but not too fast or implausibly smooth. His broader direction for Mando’s action, Hickel recalled, was “less James Bond, more Jackass” — perilous escapes that appear perpetually on the edge of disaster.

Rotta the Hutt, voiced by Jeremy Allen White, required an even bigger departure from familiar “Star Wars” imagery. Instead of Jabba’s sedentary bulk, Rotta needed to move like a powerful fighter while remaining a character audiences could sympathize with. Legacy Effects made full-size physical references, while ILM developed a digital muscle system and explored movements inspired by elephant seals and sumo wrestlers.

But after shooting, Favreau worried the original design looked too much like “Battletoads.” “He just didn’t feel Hutt-y enough,” Hickel said. “And he didn’t feel like his father’s son.” The team revised Rotta’s face and coloring to bring him closer to Jabba while refining his muscular physique. “We want you to like him, care about him, root for him,” Hickel explained. He also revealed that Rotta had the second-largest amount of dialogue after Mando, prompting the decision to have him speak English rather than require younger viewers to read extensive subtitles.

The softer side of that characterization even included an homage to Hayao Miyazaki’s “My Neighbor Totoro”: Dave Filoni drew Grogu asleep on Rotta’s chest during a production meeting. “That’s a ‘Totoro’ moment, for sure,” Hickel confirmed.

Another sequence turned the holographic chess monsters from the 1977 “Star Wars” into full-sized combatants. Tippett and fellow animator Jon Berg had originally created the miniature figures under intense deadline pressure. For the new movie, ILM preserved their recognizable silhouettes while inventing more realistic anatomy, movement and fighting styles. Meanwhile, second-unit director Peter Ramsey worked alongside stunt performers, with some creature interactions achieved through surprisingly simple physical stand-ins. “Low tech. Sometimes it’s the best tech,” Hickel quipped.

The most direct tribute to Tippett came in the battle against two giant droids guarding an overlord’s chamber. “We did an actual stop-motion sequence in this film at Tippett Studios,” Hickel added. Working with Tippett’s animators, Favreau and the editors, he turned a few script sentences into a complicated fight. “The action math on this was surprisingly complicated,” he admitted. “It kind of bent my brain at times.” Tippett’s team animated physical puppets, while ILM handled compositing and digital fire, smoke and explosions.

Hickel also found himself back behind the camera, moving a puppet frame by frame. “They made me take a shot myself,” he recalled. “I was reluctant, but I did it.”

The experience is now especially poignant: Tippett Studio has since left its longtime Berkeley facility, though the company continues operating elsewhere. “Sitting on the Tippett stage, which we all know now is no more, doing stop-motion on a ‘Star Wars’ film will probably be forever the pinnacle of my career,” Hickel said. “And I don’t mean that lightly.”

article_text:
Tom Cruise has been selected to receive the 52nd AFI Life Achievement Award. The American Film Institute will honor him at a gala tribute at the Dolby Theater in Hollywood on April 24, 2027.

Considered the highest honor for a career in film, the AFI Life Achievement Award is given to a single honoree each year, recognizing talent that has furthered the cinematic arts, demonstrated longevity and been acknowledged by scholars, critics, peers and audiences.

Related Stories

Music Industry Moves: Believe Names Adriana Sein President of Americas; Guy Moot Joins NMPA Board

Chair of the AFI Board of Trustees Kathleen Kennedy said in a statement: “Tom Cruise is a global icon. As an actor and producer, he brings an extraordinary commitment to everything he does. What I especially admire is his deep belief in movies and their ability to bring people together.” Kennedy added, “That passion has made him an extraordinary ambassador for American film around the world. It is AFI’s honor to present him with the 52nd AFI Life Achievement Award.”

Actor, producer and philanthropist Cruise has a career spanning over five decades. The three-time Oscar nominee’s films have earned nearly $13 billion in worldwide box office.

His career spans films including: “Risky Business,” “Top Gun,” “Minority Report,” “Interview With the Vampire,” “A Few Good Men,” “The Firm,” and the “Mission: Impossible” films. Cruise is currently starring in “Digger.” As previously announced , Cruise is set to star alongside Anne Hathaway in the next chapter of “ Days of Thunder ” which will be released in 2028.

He landed best actor nods for his work on “Born On The Fourth of July” and “Jerry Maguire,” and supporting actor nod for “Magnolia.” Most recently, he earned a nomination as the producer of “Top Gun: Maverick” which was nominated for best picture.

The AFI Life Achievement Award honoree is selected by the AFI Board of Trustees. Last year’s recipient was Eddie Murphy. Previous winners from the past decade include Francis Ford Coppola, Steve Martin, John Williams, Diane Keaton, George Clooney, Denzel Washington, Julie Andrews and Nicole Kidman.

article_text:
デヴィッド・ボウイがダンス作品に。鬼才マルコス・モラウ演出、2029年に東京公演決定

デヴィッド・ボウイ の 音楽 と芸術性をテーマにした新作ダンス作品『ダンス・フォー・ボウイ』の国際共同制作が発表された。演出・振付は三島由紀夫『金閣寺』舞台化も手がけたマルコス・モラウ。ボウイ本人の歌声を使用し、「変身と再生」の創造性を身体表現へと昇華させる。

デヴィッド・ボウイ の芸術世界をダンスで表現する新作『ダンス・フォー・ボウイ（SUBJECT TO CHANGE - A Dance for David Bowie）』が2029年初東京で上演される。Bunkamura、 ロンドン のサドラーズ・ウェルズ、スペインのダンスカンパニー、ラ・ヴェロナルによる国際共同制作。

演出・振付を手がけるのは、スペイン出身の振付家マルコス・モラウ。2026年夏には三島由紀夫の小説『金閣寺』を舞台化し、文楽や歌舞伎、日本の伝統音楽と現代ダンスを融合させた作品で注目を集めた。新作は2028年春にルクセンブルク市立劇場で世界初演を迎え、同年秋にはロンドンのサドラーズ・ウェルズで英国初演、2029年春には東京でアジア初演が予定されている。

本作が描くのは、ボウイの生涯をたどる伝記的な物語ではない。モラウが着目したのは、ボウイがそのキャリアを通じて繰り返した「変身」と「再生」だ。

ジギー・スターダスト、アラジン・セイン、ハロウィン・ジャック、シン・ホワイト・デューク。ボウイは次々と異なるペルソナを生み出し、 音楽 だけでなく、 ファッション や身体、アイデンティティまでも変化させながら、新たな表現を切り拓いてきた。原題の「SUBJECT TO CHANGE」には、「変更される可能性がある」「まだ決まった形ではない」という意味が込められている。

モラウはボウイについて、「芸術的な転生」を繰り返したアーティストだったと語る。ひとつのペルソナを終わらせることで次の存在を生み出し、その最後の変容が、死の直前に発表されたアルバム『ブラックスター』だったと指摘。自らの死さえも作品の一部へと変えたボウイの創造性を、音と身体によって舞台上に再構築するという。

音楽には、ボウイの代表曲と本人のオリジナル・ヴォーカルを使用。世界各地で録音される民族音楽に根差したコーラスを重ね、さらにスペインのヴォーカリスト、マリア・アルナルの歌声を交えることで、ボウイの音楽を新たな文脈へと置き直す。

制作陣には、モラウの『Notte Morricone』でも協働したアレックス・レーザー・ヴァティシェとベン・メールヴァイン（OZCUR）が作曲で参加。衣裳をシルヴィア・ドゥラニョー、舞台美術をマックス・グレンツェルが担当する。

モラウは2005年にラ・ヴェロナルを設立し、演劇、写真、映像、ダンスを横断する独自の舞台表現を展開してきた。2013年にスペイン国家舞踊賞を受賞し、2023年にはフランス芸術文化勲章シュヴァリエを受章。ドイツのダンス専門誌『tanz』では2023年と2025年に年間最優秀振付家に選出されている。

今回のプロジェクトで公開されたメインビジュアルにも、ボウイと日本のファッションの深い関係が反映されている。モチーフとなったのは、山本寛斎がデザインし、ボウイが1973年にステージで着用したことで知られる衣裳「TOKYO POP」。写真家の下村一喜が撮影を手がけ、ボウイの視覚的なレガシーを現代に蘇らせている。

音楽家であると同時に、ファッションや映画、パフォーマンスを通じて自己のイメージを絶えず更新してきたボウイ。その創造性は、ジャンルの境界を横断しながら身体表現を探究するモラウの芸術と、どのように交差するのか。

『ダンス・フォー・ボウイ』の東京公演は2029年春を予定。会場やチケット情報などの詳細は今後発表される。

title_original: Dans « Low Expectations » d’Eivind Landsvik, girl in red trouve un premier rôle touchant
editorial_title_zh: 在埃文·兰斯维克（Eivind Landsvik）的《Low Expectations》中，girl in red奉献了动人的银幕首秀
editorial_excerpt_zh: 这部关于年轻女音乐人抑郁症的剧情片，身披现代挪威电影的外衣（现实主义与流行忧郁），听觉与情感均恰到好处。音乐人girl in red在此迎来了她首个优质的电影主角。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://www.troiscouleurs.fr/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/496be15830c801e2260f290261bff31c-1024x510.webp", "alt": "496be15830c801e2260f290261bff31c", "caption": "", "credit": "Trois Couleurs", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她的抑郁症吞噬了一切，所以干脆选择不表现出来。作为这部挪威电影的次要元素，玛雅（Maja）的心理状态摒弃了心理剧情片中常见的许多噱头，转而用来标记她对生活的勃勃生机。在经历了音乐领域的爆发式职业生涯（艺名为Vongole，这是一个可以想见既有趣又时髦的项目）、创意上的燃尽以及对各类非法物质的过度消耗之后，这位年轻女子回到了母亲身边，做着一份高中看守的零工。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "巧妙的眩晕感在于，玛雅由玛丽·乌尔文·林海姆（Marie Ulven Ringheim）饰演，也就是我们更为熟知的艺名：girl in red。但影片有着很好的克制，没有把一切混为一谈，而是与她的音乐保持了一定距离——尽管《Low Expectations》听起来本身就带有当事人的风格：温柔而有力。整体而言，它自然带有这种空灵而忧郁的挪威电影风格，令人联想到达格·约翰·豪格鲁德（Dag Johan Haugerud，2025年旋转的《梦想·爱情·欲望》）或约阿希姆·特里尔（Joachim Trier）的作品（当我们看到《奥斯陆，8月31日》里的安德斯·丹尼尔森·李被拍摄、被老去的方式时，《Low Expectations》几乎变得有些元叙事了），但它更加脚踏其isSignedIn地气，顺应时代潮流。它围绕着这个常规却又根本的问题展开评论：在29岁的时候，我们是否可以开始怀疑自己是不是把人生过砸了？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "埃文·兰斯维克（Eivind Landsvik）的《Low Expectations》，UFO发行（1 h 45），10月14日上映", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "关注我们", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Sa dépression consume tout, alors autant ne pas le montrer. Élément secondaire de ce film norvégien qui exclut de sa mise en scène bien des gimmicks du drame psychologique, l’état psychique de Maja ponctuera plutôt ses élans de vie. La jeune femme est de retour chez sa mère avec un petit boulot de surveillante de lycée, après une carrière explosive dans la musique (sous le nom de Vongole, projet que l’on devine fun et hype) et un burn-out créatif – plus des excès de consommations diversement illicites.

Habile vertige, Maja est jouée par Marie Ulven Ringheim, que l’on connaît plutôt sous son nom de scène : girl in red. Mais le film a le bon goût de ne pas tout confondre et tient sa musique à distance – même si Low Expectations sonne déjà comme un morceau de l’intéressée : doux et puissant. L’ensemble est bien sûr à l’image de ce cinéma norvégien éthéré et mélancolique à la mode Dag Johan Haugerud (les tourbillonnants Rêves, Amour, Désir de 2025) ou Joachim Trier ( Low Expectations devient presque méta quand on voit la manière dont est filmé, vieilli, l’Anders Danielsen Lie d’ Oslo, 31 août ), mais reste plus terre à terre, dans l’air du temps. Glosant autour de cette question conventionnelle mais fondamentale : peut-on, à 29 ans, se demander si on a raté sa vie ?

Low Expectations d’Eivind Landsvik , UFO (1 h 45) , sortie le 14 octobre

article_text:
Audiences continued to flock to “ You Can See Everything ,” as the twisty documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes captured the zeitgeist and saw its grosses increase in its second weekend. The A24 film earned $19.5 million over its sophomore frame, a 25% improvement from its $15.6 million opening. Few movies see their grosses rise like that.

However, the film expanded its theater count, which helped lift ticket sales. “You Can See Everything” is playing in 2,655 theaters, up from the 855 it debuted on the previous weekend. Its popularity is remarkable considering that “You Can See Everything” is a three-hour documentary that is playing like a broadly commercial feature. It helped that A24 cloaked the film in secrecy , convincing audiences that the only way to avoid spoilers was to buy a ticket.

Produced for a mere $7 million, “You Can See Everything” has grossed $45.1 million, positioning it to be one of the most successful non-fiction films in history. Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11,” an anti-Bush treatise released in the midst of the contentious 2004 presidential election, remains the highest-grossing documentary with just over $222 million in receipts. “You Can See Everything” has easily topped “Melania,” which had been the year’s highest-grossing doc with its $16.3 million gross. That look at the gilded life of America’s First Lady was a lot less profitable given that Jeff Bezos and Amazon MGM Studios shelled out $40 million for the rights (they love non-fiction filmmaking!).

Will the box office success propel “You Can See Everything” and its directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim into the Oscar race? The jury is still out on that, though awards prognosticators have written many , many , many words on the subject.

Even if the documentary branch shuts Fielder and Oppenheim out or “You Can See Everything” fails to be the first documentary to land a Best Picture nomination, it will go down as a massive hit for A24, extending a sizzling streak at the box office. This year, the studio released “Backrooms,” the biggest blockbuster in its history with a $400 million global haul, as well as winners like “Primetime” and “The Drama.” And it did by proving that audiences will turn up in theaters for more than just superhero flicks and sequels. Turns out, they’re interested in Silicon Valley flameouts too.
excerpt_original: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's twisty look at Elizabeth Holmes saw its grosses increase from its red-hot debut.
